19.2          Merger of DSP and ASP
 
The Committee views thatthe close proximity of Alloy Steels Plant and Durgapur Steel Plant, under the same
organisations – SAIL, is a matter of great advantage. ASP is utilizing scrap skull, C. O. gas, electricity,  water, dolomite,
oxygen from DSP.  It also utilises Hot Metal/Liquid Steel, Ingot, Blooms & Billets as input materials. The two sister
plants of SAIL are having common township and Hospital, under the control of same Managing Director. Therefore ,
the Committee feels that the possibility of merger of DSP and ASP may be explored . This plant could be made more
cost effective by utilizing the in-house facilities of the two SAIL Plants, ASP & DSP. This requires  more close
supervision and effective co-ordination. This should not be a difficult job since the two plants are under the control of
same Managing Director.  What is needed, is the will of SAIL to run both the Plants, making best use of the technical
arrangements already prevailing to make both the Plants economically viable.
 
19.3     The suggestion of R&D, SAIL, to install an AOD at ASP for improving quality of stainless steel and EMS at
concast shop for production of Defence & Automobile requirements, should be examined The other suggestion of
technical experts like Dastur & Co. to install a Billet Caster, Wire Rod Mill and modernize the Forge Shop , may be
taken into  consideration .
 
19.4     The Sub-Committee was apprised of the fact that after installation of continuous shop in various steel plants, the
availability of mild steel scrap has drastically gone down.  ASP's requirement of scrap from different plants is 10,000
MT per month.  Following is the need from sister plants to sustain production level.
            1. Bokaro Steel Plant :   4500 MT
            2. Durgapur Steel Plant:    5500 MT
19.5     The special steels produced in integrated steel plant is very cost effective.  In ASP, is also exploring the
possibility of getting the inputs from Durgapur Steel Plant in the form of ingots/Basic Oxygen Furnace Liquid
steel/Rolled or Cast Billet & Blooms to the tune of 6000 MT per month.  At present it is at the level of 1500 T per
month. This is being perused at various levels in SAIL and  they  are sure to get this support within SAIL.
 
19.6
          Utilizing inputs from DSP like liquid steel  
 
The Committee is of the view that  to reduce the cost of production of ASP products, a substantial quantity of
ASP customer’s need can be meted out by utilizing inputs from DSP like liquid steel made through BOF route as well as
Ingots, Bloom and Billets.  The Committee hopes production of ASP may be carried on  with close co-ordination with
Durgapur Steel Plant.  With transfer of liquid steel from DSP to the tune of yearly 50,000 MT monthly 4500 MT.  To
facilitate the transfer of this Steel, necessary arrangement may  be made.
 
19.7          Installation of two numbers of E.M.S. in the CCS
 
The  installation of two numbers of E.M.S. in the CCS, which is essential for regaining lost market in the
automobile sectors of the Eastern Region , may be examined.
 
19.8     Use of DSP-ASP route
Electric Arc Steel making is a costly process which should   be sparingly used  at  ASP.  ASP should utilize
ASP's finishing facilities to produce around 90,000 tonnes of steel from DSP-ASP route per annum to make a cost
effective contribution.

ASP has a large potential in production of high quality  forgings   upto 12,000  TPA.  A nominal   investment to

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
 
Operational Status of Alloy Steel Plant (ASP)
 
            The   Committee believes that the Secretary, Ministry of Steel has reasons to express concern over the
operational status of Alloy Steel Plant (ASP)  .  ASP is facing all odds.  The plant has suffered huge accumulated loss, is
incapable of utilising installed capacity and facilities available, scale of production is unviable, financial performance  is
dwindling,  cost of production is uncompetitive   and it has lost its market.  The disinvestment effect failed as `
Expression of  Interest'  (EOI )  has   evoked  no   response.  Government agencies are not coming forward to help the
plant out.  The performance of plant in the past has been gloomy and at presents the plant is at moribund stage.  The
Committee is of the opinion that the plant may reach to the  point of no return unless a comprehensively considered
revival package is undertaken  to improve the operational efficiency   of the plant under  guided   supervision  for the
ultimate survival  and  sustenance of the plant.
( Para : 1.4)
Capital Structure
            The Committee is perturbed to note the huge accumulated loss of ASP.  The huge accumulated loss i.e. to the
tune of Rs. 1184.00 crores is a testimony to the fact that the pervious management failed to act promptly.
( Para :  2.3   )
Facilities available at ASP
            The Committee, while noting the facilities available at ASP, is constrained to express its concern over the under-
utilisation of facilities available at ASP.  Reasons for under-utilisation may be of different nature, i.e. varying   from
general recession in steel industry to specific and inherent problems of plant. Some of the   reasons might seems
justified   and might be well defended by   stating that, factors forming the reasons, were beyond the control of
management, the other reasons might be pointed out, could be dwindling market demand   of  ASP's  product.  However,
the   facts remains that   elaborate facilities is available at ASP and expansion programme   in ASP was completed as
late as March, 1988 and   infrastructure facilities of the plant has   since been expanded from 1,60,000 tpa to 2,60,000
tpa of liquid Steel and 1,83,000.  The Committee is perturbed to observe that investment on expansion projects in ASP
was made without proper techno-economic consideration. Expansion projects in ASP were bereft of cost-benefits
analysis, the Committee feels.
( Para : 3.3  )
Product Range
 
            The Committee feels that, since ASP  has elaborate facilities, it is but natural that the plant has the  basic
facilities to produce wide range of products  for a number of customers such as Engineering, Railways, Defence and
Automobile Sector.  But the irony of state of affairs in ASP is that the facilities available at ASP is gathering  dust and
the  wide  range  of products available  at ASP remained a mere expression on paper ,  as the so-called esteemed 
customers  of  ASP has turned their back to the  ASP product due to cost  disadvantages.  Therefore, the production in
ASP has, accordingly, been confined as per market demand.
( Para :  4.3   )
Scale of Production

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/111threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:26:00]
            The Committee is of the opinion that the production level in ASP is, itself an indicator to the fact as how
improper planning in regard to enhancing the ASP 's capacity  from 1,60,000 tpa  to 2,60,000  tpa of liquid steel and
1,83,000  tonnes of saleable steel in March, 1988 led to misappropriation  of public  purse.  The plant failed to make
optimum   utilisation of installed capacity, the Committee observes.  Its a glaring example  of error of judgement.  It
might be well concluded that the  then decision -makers and the management  made a  blunder and  went  for the 
expansion  programme without  taking  into consideration the  techno-economic viability of the  plant.
( Para :  5.3 )
Sales performance
 
            The Committee observes that the plant has the capacity of  making 1,83,000 tonnes of saleable steel but the
actual sales remained confined to 134.9, 96.00 and 80.6 thousand tonnes during 1998-99, 1999-2000 and 2001-02,
respectively, which raises  a question mark on the economic  prudence  of decision maker of the time.  During 2001-02,
ASP is likely to sell 85,00 tonnes of Alloy Steel against rated capacity of  1,83,000 tonnes which works out to be 46
percent  .  The major orders received from PSUs  by ASP are  from Railway, Defence, BHEL, and steel plants.  In the
recent past, Railway and Defence,  have both curtailed their procurement and they are resourcing  their  requirement
from supplies other than PSUs also.
( Para : 6.2 )
Financial Performance of ASP
 
            The Committee views that, it is but  natural, that a plant which is not making optimum utilisation of facilities
available at site, neither  makes  full use of its installed capacity and which has  lost its market, can not  be expected to
perform better  on the financial   front.  ASP is incurring losses year after year and there is  no hope left  for
improvement in its performance, as the plant faces  indomitable problems.  The Committee is  of the  further view that
Government should make a final decision in regard to ASP at the earliest   as ASP is proving a burden  on public purse.

            The reasons, as advocatd by the Ministry of Steel for deteriorating physical and financial performance of ASP,
makes the Committee to recall the proverb that  "misfortune never comes alone ", as the prevailing  conditions  in ASP
are  the major  stumbling block  for better  functioning of the plant.  The Plant, in itself , is in a dilapidated    condition 
and the Committee is dismayed, not only for the dwindling financial performance of ASP  but also for the  plant which
is gradually  but surely marching   towards sad demise.
( Para : 7.5  )
Cost of Production
 
            The Committee recommends that ASP management may undertake massive measures for cost-reduction  in the
production of the items
( Para : 8.3  )
Cost control measure
 
            The Committee appreciates the efforts made by ASP management for making a savings of Rs.5.00 crore during
2000-01.  The Committee hopes that such efforts would continue in future.
( Para : 9.2 )
Major problems faced by ASP and solution:
 
            The Committee observes that the problems being faced by ASP are deeply- rooted and pose the real threat for
the survival and sustenance of the   plant   under the prevailing environment.  There are the   reasons to believe that
ASP  plant is fundamentally  un-competitive because of its location, (ASP has  a business   disadvantage  vis-à-vis its
competitors  because  of its location in the   eastern region, while    nearly 60%  of the market demand is from Southern
and  Western regions  and  therefore, ASP has a freight cost  disadvantages vis-a-vis  a south based suppliers),  low
quality  of assets  and mounting  loss and liability ( against a net  fixed assets  of Rs.130.00 crore and current assets of
Rs.242.00 crores,   the plant has the  current liabilities to the tune of  Rs.212.00  crores and huge  accumulated loss to
the extent of Rs.1184.00 crore),   outdated-technology                      ( uneconomical  low  power EAF  route)  and

decreasing sales realisation.  And since SAIL, itself,  is passing through  rough financial phase and its financial
performance, itself is  uncomfortable, SAIL is not coming forward for the  rescuing  act  of ASP.

Market Prospect of ASP
 
 
            The Committee recommends that ASP management for enhancing its market share may undertake concrete
efforts.  SAIL should help ASP in procurement of work-order from Railway, Defence, BHEL and other Steel plant.

            The Committee notes   the budgetary provision for ASP as earmarked for 2002-03 and hopes that schemes

Financial Requirement For Upgradation of Technology
 
 
            The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should examine the proposal of upgradation of
technology after taking into consideration the Cost-Benefit Analysis and, if the study    favours,  the  Ministry of  Steel
may  facilitate ASP for  arranging  required  fund either from SAIL, on commercial borrowings on Government's 
guarantee.

Rationalisation of Manpower
 
            The Committee feels that rationalisation of manpower is   an absolute necessity in ASP    to reduce the element
of labour-cost component.  The programme of rationalisation of manpower should be completed in a time bound
manner and without any delay.
( Para : 14.5  )
SWOT ( Strength, Weakness, Opportunities, Threats)  analysis of ASP
 
            The Committee feels that ASP has failed, miserably, in taking advantage   of its strength , at appropriate time . 
ASP is not in a position to avail of its opportunities because of high cost of production as the finishing   facilities are not
cost   effective which   put ACP at disadvantage in matching international   cost and quality in the production of 
stainless steel and  other steel plants  are producing carbon construction steel at a lower cost.  Taking stock of SWOT  -
analysis , the Committee is of the opinion that the plant is heading towards a point of no  return.
( Para :  15.2 )
Disinvestment  of ASP
 
            The Committee understands that, considering ASP's financial performance in the past and no strong possibility
of improvement, in future ASP is proving a nuisance to SAIL's  in general and burden on government's treasure. 
Therefore, efforts were made for divestment of ASP.  However, market proved much more prudent and Expression of
Interest (EOI) evoked   no response for purchasing the ailing plant of SAIL.  ASP is dwindling further, SAIL is not in a
position to invest  , and Government   is not in a position to inject `new lease of life ' to the plant, which seems to be at
the  moribund stage.
( Para : 16.2 )

            Issue  of transfer of Alloy Steels  Plant to Department of Defence Production & Supplies.
( Para :17.0)
 
            In a bid to disown the ailing ASP, the Ministry of Steel, once made efforts for the transfer of ASP to the
Department of Defence (  Production & Supplies) on the logic  that ASP was  conceived  and developed, in early sixties,
to cater to the needs of various sectors of industry, especially Defence and Special scientific  application   like nuclear
power plant.  The Department of Defence production & supplies declined to take over ASP in view of that fact that the
total annual  requirement of  all   kinds  of steel , by ordinance factory  board of Ministry of Defence , is only  a very
small fraction (21 percent )  of the total production of Alloy.  The Committee finds ASP between the devil and the  deep
sea, as it has no taker and the  present  one  is willing to disown it.  The Committee feels that its hardly matters whether 
ASP is under the administrative   control of Ministry of  Steel or the Department of  Defence( Production and Supplies),
and what actually  matters is the question of   the  survival of ASP and the future  prospects of the plant.

            The Committee recommends that any capital investment in ASP   be made after taking into consideration the

Austerity measures
 
            The Committee welcomes the steps undertaken by SAIL/ Ministry of Steel for revival of ASP. The Committee

The Committee is of the opinion that Alloy Steels Plant is a  pioneer in the production of stainless steel in India,
and   its products are  being  used by the Defence, Railway, Space Research Organisations, Nuclear Power Plants .
When India was debarred to import alloy steels required for Bofors Cannon Shells during Kargil conflict and high
quality special stainless steel required for  Atomic Research Centres ,after the Nuclear Test at Pokhran, it was ASP,
which  came forward to produce all these materials required at the moment of national crisis. Therefore, the Committee
feels that It would  be a national loss if ASP, a holder of ISO-9002 Certificate , is thrown away.
( Para : 19.1)
 
Merger of DSP and ASP
 
The Committee views thatthe close proximity of Alloy Steels Plant and Durgapur Steel Plant, under the same
organisations – SAIL, is a matter of great advantage. ASP is utilizing scrap skull, C. O. gas, electricity,  water, dolomite,
oxygen from DSP.  It also utilises Hot Metal/Liquid Steel, Ingot, Blooms & Billets as input materials. The two sister
plants of SAIL are having common township and Hospital, under the control of same Managing Director. Therefore ,
the Committee feels that the possibility of merger of DSP and ASP may be explored . This plant could be made more
cost effective by utilizing the in-house facilities of the two SAIL Plants, ASP & DSP. This requires  more close
supervision and effective co-ordination. This should not be a difficult job since the two plants are under the control of
same Managing Director.  What is needed, is the will of SAIL to run both the Plants, making best use of the technical
arrangements already prevailing to make both the Plants economically viable.
( Para :  19.3)
 
            The suggestion of R&D, SAIL, to install an AOD at ASP for improving quality of stainless steel and EMS at

taken into  consideration .

Utilizing inputs from DSP like liquid steel  
 
The Committee is of the view that  to reduce the cost of production of ASP products, a substantial quantity of
ASP customer’s need can be meted out by utilizing inputs from DSP like liquid steel made through BOF route as well as
Ingots, Bloom and Billets.  The Committee hopes production of ASP may be carried on  with close co-ordination with
Durgapur Steel Plant.  With transfer of liquid steel from DSP to the tune of yearly 50,000 MT monthly 4500 MT.  To
facilitate the transfer of this Steel, necessary arrangement may  be made.
 
Installation of two numbers of E.M.S. in the CCS
 
The  installation of two numbers of E.M.S. in the CCS, which is essential for regaining lost market in the
automobile sectors of the Eastern Region , may be examined.

Electric Arc Steel making is a costly process which should   be sparingly used  at  ASP.  ASP should utilize

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS  WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
Recommendations ( Para  4.2  )  
 
Objectives of Modernisation.
                       
   The Committee understands that since DSP was facing problems of poor quality of raw materials, obsolete technology
and inadequate air pollution control measures which necessitated that it undertake the modernisation projects. The
Committee, while noting the objective of modernisation, hopes that DSP Management would make every effort for
achieving the objectives of modernisation during its stabilisation phase.
 
 
Action Taken
            DSP management is making every effort for achieving the objectives of modernisation.  Hot metal  production in
Durgapur Steel Plant has increased from 1138000 Tonne  in 1987-88 (Pre-modernisation) to 881000 Tonne in 2002-
03 (April-September).
                      
Recommendations ( Para 11.3  )
 
Further Modernisation and Restructuring for technology Upgradation
 
   The Committee recommends that the DSP management should push ahead, without delay, the issue of further
upgradation in DSP in regard to Bloom Caster with ladle furnace, New Finishing Mill, Introduction of coal dust
injection and Introduction of SGP for BF-2 for revenue generation and improvement in environment.  The Committee
hopes that SAIL and the Ministry of Steel would extend its helping hand to DSP.
 
Action Taken
            During 10 th Five Year Plan, it has been envisaged that among other schemes for DSP, the proposal for
installation of Wire Rod Mill, Bloom Caster with Ladle furnace and Installation of Slag Granulation Plant in BF-2
would be considered depending upon funds availability and techno-economics. Presently, Installation of Wire Rod Mill
is being considered.
 
Recommendations ( Para  12.2   )
  Conversion of CC Billets into finished products.
 
The Committee understands that almost 55 percent of DSP’s production comprises of semis, which are low contributory
items and fetch lower realization.  The product-mix of DSP is unfavourable and is affecting the profitability of DSP. 
The Committee recommends that DSP Management should chalk out a necessary course of plan for converting CC
Billets into finished products through conversion agents.  The Committee hopes that SAIL should lend its helping hand
to DSP management in chalking out the plan and proposing the same to Ministry of Steel, as the same would help DSP
in improving its physical and financial performance.

 Completion of  AMR scheme without time and cost over-run

without time and cost over-run.

  SWOT  ANALYSIS
 
The Committee is of the opinion that since DSP has acquired State of the – Art Technology, including the
benefits of high degree of computerization and automation, it would be able to improve its working and performance,
thereby marching ahead towards achieving the goal of a profit making plant.
 
Action Taken
            Durgapur Steel Plant has started making cash profits since 2000-01.  During April’ 02 to Sep’02  (1 st Half of
2002 – 03),  the plant has made a cash profit of Rs. 10  crore.  Recommendations ( Para    14.4 )  
SWOT  ANALYSIS
The Committee, while appreciating the steps taken by DSP management for reducing the cost of production,
feels that DSP management may capitalise the introduction of CDI in the modernised Blast Furnace for further
reduction in input cost of coal.  The Committee is hopeful that DSP management taking advantage of modernised steel

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS  WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
Recommendations ( Para  6.2 )  
 
Long-term Corporate Plan of RINL
 
The Committee notes the long-term Corporate Plan of RINL to increase its capacity to 10 million tonnes
(envisaging production of 7.0 million tonnes by 2013-14 and 10 million tonnes by 2019-20) with addition of production
units in both primary and finishing zones.  In this context, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should
examine the proposal of RINL management to enhance the  capacity of the plant and, if found feasible, the Ministry of
Steel should help RINL management   for arranging commercial borrowings.  However, it may be noted that the
capacity  expansion programme in steel sector should be well examined, keeping in view of  prevailing over supply in
steel market.  Therefore, the expansion programme  should be backed by intensification of diversification of product
range in order to be a dominant player in the market.
 
Action Taken
 
Ministry notes the observation of the Committee and will look at further capacity expansion of VSP, hoping the
national and international demand for its products and its long term interests.
 
Recommendations ( Para 7.5   ) 
 
RINL- On the profit- making track
 
The Committee observes that RINL is gradually,  but surely, marching ahead on the profit making track.  The
plant is already in the position of making cash profit and the Committee hopes that the plant, with excellent capacity
utilisation  and skilled and devoted work force, would soon start making net profit.
 
Action Taken
 
The Ministry notes the observations of the Committee and wishes to inform the Committee that as per tentative
financial results available for the first half of the current financial year the company has already registered a net profit of
Rs.125 crores. 
 
Recommendations ( Para 7.6  )  
 
Operational efficiency of RINL
 
                        The Committee recommends that RINL managements should intensify its efforts i.e., increase in
operational efficiency, enhance in capacity utilisation, adopt cost control measures, widen market network to improve
physical and financial performance of the  plant.
 
Action Taken
 
 Ministry and the company note the  recommendations of the Committee for implementation.   The Committee is
also informed that RINL management has been pursuing the goal of achieving high operational efficiencies,

enhancement of capacity utilization, cost control and expansion of market network.   The positive impact of these
measures is visible in the improved physical and financial performance of the company in the first half of the current
financial year. 
 
Recommendations ( Para10.4 )
 
AMR scheme OF RINL
 
The Committee opines that AMR scheme is essential for running the production units, as a continuous basis, at
their rated capacity.   The Committee is pleased to note that RINL is capable of making investment on AMR projects
through IEBR and nogovernment support is required for the purpose.   However, the Committee recommends that all
AMR schemes should be completed without time and cost overruns.
 
Action Taken
 
 Ministry and the Company note the recommendations of the Committee.
 
Recommendations ( Para 13.4  )
 
Proposal of long-term Comprehensive Turnaround Package
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that, since RINL has started to make cash profit and is poised to make net profit
by 2003-04, an opportunity should be given for turnaround.   The Committee observes that the proposal of long-term
Comprehensive Turnaround Package has long been under the consideration of Government.   The contention of the
Ministry of Finance, that, the expansion programme, at this stage, would only lead RINL to increased losses, is without
substance and logic, in view of the resurrection of the company (gearing up of the company to make profit) and
improving the steel scenario in general.   And when there no surplus manpower in RINL, there is no reason for adopting
VRS.   The Committee feels that the comprehensive turnaround plan should have got the nod of the Government for
ensuring the viability of the company.   RINL has got excellent lay out, effective and efficient management and devoted
workers.   The company may prove an anchor sheet of India Steel Industry.   The Comprehensive, Turnaround package
as prepared by M/s A.T. Kearney & MECON had the sound attributes for the revival of the company i.e. initiation of
action to create Holding company structure as an independent subsidiary to be styled as an infrastructure company; and
diversification of existing products-mix and enhancement of capacity to 4.0 million tonnes production with a investment
of Rs.1742 crore.   The revival plan also included raising of capital for funding the project and for repayment of debt
and interest.   That is why, the Committee, in its 30 th Report (On Demands for Grants 1999-2000), 37 th Report (on
Demands for Grants 1999-2000), 51 st Report (on Demands for Grants, 2001-02) and 70 th Report (on Demands for
Grants 2002-03) recommended the Government for giving the due consideration to the comprehensive turn around
proposal of RINL.  But, of no avail, track, and the only thing required is the one time assistance from the Government. 
Once the revival package is cleared by theGovernment, the plant would start running with appreciable acceleration, the
Committee hopes.  
 
Recommendations ( Para 14.5 )
 
Short term turnaround proposal for revival of RINL.  
 
The Committee recommends that the Government should not hesitate in clearing the short term turnaround
proposal for revival of RINL.   The Committee is in agreement with the argument of RINL management that, setting of
accumulated losses of Rs.4981 crore (Provisional) as on 31 st March, 2002 against the preference share capital of
Rs.2937  crore and balance against equity capital, would not entail any cash outgo for the Government of India but
would definitely strengthen the balance sheet of the company.

Recommendations ( Para 17.4  )  
 
Price  determined by the free market forces of demand and supply
 
            The Committee opines that, in a liberal economy, price is determined by the free market forces of demand and
supply.  Strength of the competitors sets the motion of the market.   Therefore, in order to dominate the market one has
to be watchful and alert to have full and current knowledge of market forces.   The Committee is pleased to note that
RINL has the pricing cell in the marketing Department which collects the market related information like market price,
the quantum of demand and scale of supply of the products, competition prices, etc and the same is communicated to the
decision-makers.   The Committee recommends that adequate market research should be undertaken by the market wing
of RINL and, thereafter, system of market-related forecasting like demand trend, quantum of supply product-mix etc.
may be worked out in order to emerge a leader and manager of the market.   Quick decision making mechanism for
marketing purpose is a key to success.
 
Recommendations ( Para 17.8 ) 
 
 Consumer’s satisfaction.
 
The Committee is of the opinion that in a liberal and globalised economy customers is the king of market.  
Therefore, RINL management’s first and the foremost motto should be consumer’s satisfaction.  Meeting of customer’s
requirement in time should be the guiding principle of RINL’s management.   The marketing wing of RINL should
undertake measures for taking new market zones in India and abroad.

 Ultimate meta-goal of a corporate body

EXPORT CREDIT GURANTEE CORPORATION
 
1.1            RECOMMENDATION  (PARA 6.1)
 
 
            The Committee is of the view that ECGC should expand the range of its activities to cater to medium and small-scale
exporters. The Committee recommends that ECGC should endeavor towards specialization based on customer segmentation
based on customer size, which has become a necessity in the present circumstances.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The recommendation of the Committee will be brought to the notice of the management of the ECGC and the
Administrative Ministry for their consideration.

1.2            RECOMMENDATION (PARA 6.2)
 
The Committee after examining the performance of ECGC within the MOU parameters is of the opinion that
weightage should be given to the role played by ECGC in providing impetus to exports in the small-scale sector. The
Committee feels that the SSI sector makes a marked presence in the export market and comprises a part 45 percent of the
India`s exports. The Committee strongly recommends that ECGC should introduce some special scheme to promote exports
from the SSI sector.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The recommendation of the Committee is noted and the matter will be taken up with the PSE as well as with the
Administrative Ministry.
1.3            RECOMMENDATION (PARA 6.3)
 
            The Committee during the course of the deliberations felt that the customer requirements are changing and demand
for cost effective and efficient service on global standards is growing. The Committee strongly recommends that ECGC
should take immediate steps to become a strong customer oriented organization.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The PSE will be advised to take due note of the recommendation of the Committee  while formulating its long-term
policy.
 
1.4            RECOMMENDATION (PARA 6.4)
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the total exposure in terms of maximum liability underwritten by ECGC  is
disproportionate to the present capital base of ECGC. The Committee recommends that ECGC should undertake a cost
benefit analysis and a risk factor analysis so as to ensure that the liabilities do not harm the future prospects of ECGC.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The recommendation of the Committee will be brought to the notice of Administrative Ministry and the PSE for
taking necessary action in this regard.
 
1.5            RECOMMENDATION (PARA 6.5)
 
             The Committee also feels ECGC should start diversifying into new services like Export Insurance, Force Maseure
Insurance for exports etc. and also gear up to competition from Private Insurance Companies in these services.
 
ACTION TAKEN

            The Committee was of the opinion that in today’s world the impact of mass media is tremendous, however
commercial considerations should not be the sole criteria for production of films. The Committee strongly feels that films,
which are socially relevant must get preference in NFDC.

The recommendation of the Committee will be conveyed to the NFDC and to the Administrative Ministry for
necessary action.

            The Committee during the course of deliberations was of the opinion that NFDC should play a more active role
towards the popularization of Indian Cinema at the international level. The Committee recommends that NFDC should
provide support to both Indian films and Indian Directors to enable them to get international exposure and success.

The recommendation will be communicated to the Ministry and the PSE for taking action at their level.

            The Committee is of the considered opinion that the film festivals being organized by NFDC are mainly held in major
metropolitan cities. The Committee recommends that film festivals should be held in smaller towns so as to propagate and
promote Indian cinema and to provide wider audience.

            The Committee feels that NFDC should help in promoting regional films so as to enable them to get all India
viewership. The Committee recommends that NFDC should help in the distribution/exhibition of regional films by providing
Hindi/English subtitles.

 CHAPTER – I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE
GOVERNMENT
 
 
HARASSMENT OF DEFAULTING CEMENT UNITS
 
1.1       Recommendations  
 
Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation portfolio has, at present, 48 cement  manufacturing units.  Out of 48 units only 2
units are regular in payment whereas 1 unit has recently gone in production.  As per the study conducted by the Uttar
Pradesh Finance Corporation, these units are facing problems relating to market recession like in transportation cost, wage
cost, ban on mining, unimplemented units, temporary default, etc.  The Committee notes the plethora of problems being
faced   by the cement units.  In the circumstances, the Committee observes that the reported harassment of these units,
instead of reviving them by the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, as mentioned by the Association, needs to be looked
into.
(Para 5.10)
Action Taken
 
UPFC has submitted that there is no harassment of the defaulting cement units by the Corporation.  The Corporation
has been trying to contact every unit for One Time Settlement (OTS). The fact is that with the existing sale price of the
cement, none of the small scale units would be viable. The Corporation is of the view that though there has been
improvement in the demand of cement all over the country, the sales realization per bag has not improved. Even if such
units come into production they would not be able to break even and repay the Corporation’s dues. It would be in the
interest of the borrower to settle the dues of the Corporation through One Time Settlement only.
            Under the refinance scheme, SIDBI does not usually interfere with the decision on individual cases by PLIs
including SFCs.  Specific cases, if referred to, SIDBI may look into it in consultation with UPFC.
 
REVIVAL OF SICK SSI UNITS
1.2       Recommendation    
 
The Committee also notes that as per norms specified by the Reserve Bank of India, a sick unit is considered as
potentially viable, if it would be in a position, after implementing a relief package spread over a period not exceeding five
years from the commencement of the package from banks, financial institutions, Government (Central/State) and other
concerned agencies, as may be necessary, to continue to service its repayment obligations as agreed upon including those
forming part of the package, without the help of the concessions after the aforesaid period.  The repayment period of
restructuring debts should not exceed seven years from the date of implementation of the package.
(Para 6.5)
Action Taken
 
The Reserve Bank of India has issued revised, detailed, transparent and non-discretionary guidelines for
rehabilitation of current, sick and potentially viable Small Scale Industrial units, based on the recommendation of the Kohli
Committee, on 16th January, 2002.  Any proposal of revival, eligible under the above revised scheme, is examined by the
financing bank and necessary action taken, thereon.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN

THE DEMAND OF CEMENT  
 
2.1       Recommendation  
 
            The study report further mentioned that the immediate future is not very encouraging. However, once the
Government starts the revival of the economy through investment in infrastructure and construction activity picks up, the
demand for cement will grow.
(Para 5.3)
Action Taken
 
With the indications of revival of the economy in the recent months and growth in economic activity including
investments in housing and infrastructure sector, per capita consumption of cement is likely to go up driving such growth of
demand for cement with increasing GDP.
 
HARASSMENT OF DEFAULTING CEMENT UNITS
 
2.2       Recommendation    
 
            The Central Government had announced in the 8 th Five Year Plan about construction of double express highway,
houses for millions, generation of power to take the electricity to the rural areas.  Had such activities relating to
infrastructure building arisen the present state of low intake of Cement would not have arisen.  In fact, market demand of
cement was not in line with the Government’s projection.  In subsequent budgets of the Central Government the above
schemes did not find place, resulting in decline in demand of Cement.
(Para 5.11)
 
Action Taken 
 
There has been a growing thrust on infrastructure in  each subsequent budget and policy announcements. The Prime
Minister’s announcements in 1998 to construct 2 million houses annually during the 9 th Five Year Plan and to construct
concrete roads connecting the four mega cities covering around 6000 kms under the project- “ Golden Quadrilateral” and “
North-South, East-West Expressways” are significant. Implementation of such projects is likely to contribute to growth of
cement demand. 
 
ASSISTANCE TO GIANT CEMENT INDUSTRIES
 
2.3
       Recommendation      
 
The giant units which take 5-6 years to produce cement started production in 1996 in UP after taking financial
assistance from IDBI on easy terms and flooded the market with cement at a cheaper rate and ousted smaller units by
waging an unfair and unequal competition. Had the development work regarding building up infrastructure started before
1992  or during 1992-96 the smaller units would have survived and established themselves.
(Para 5.12)
Action Taken
 
            IDBI had extended assistance to companies such as Mysore Cements Ltd., for setting up a 0.5 million tons per
annum grinding unit at Jhansi, U.P. (Rs. 7.3 crore @  17.5% p.a. in 1987 and further Rs. 3 crore @ 19.5% p.a. for
modernization of the unit in 1992), Birla Corporation for setting up 0.4 million tons per annum  at Rae Bareli  (Rs. 40 crore
@ 16.25% p.a. in September, 1998) and to ACC for setting up a 0.6 million tons per annum  grinding unit at Tikaria, U.P.
(Rs. 40 crore @ 15.5% p.a. in 1998).
IDBI has not extended any soft loans to its assisted cement companies in UP. The assistance has been granted as per
the extant guidelines of IDBI prevailing at that time.

 CHAPTER – III
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT
ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
EFFECT OF RISE IN COST OF POWER COUPLED WITH BORROWING COST ON THE
CEMENT INDUSTRY
 
3.1       Recommendation    
 
            Uttar Pradesh Financial Corporation made a study regarding mini cement plants financed by the Corporation. The
study report inter-alia  mentioned that the performance of the cement industry is closely linked with the industrial growth of
the country. In the period from 1993-94 to 1995-96, when the industrial growth was higher, the scenario in the segment was
bright. In 1995-96 with 11.7% industrial growth, the cement production grew at 10.6%. As the industry slowed down in
1996-97, so did the cement segment. The same downward trend continued in 1998-99. According to the industry sources,
the current take-off position is inadequate to generate more profits, as the low price realization is still not matching the
production cost. The recession in construction activity, low investment in major infrastructure projects, rise in the cost of
power etc. coupled with high borrowing cost has marked down the industry’s earnings.
(Para 5.1)
 
Action Taken
 
            The growth of cement industry was affected due to slowdown in the industrial growth and general economic
recession.
            Regarding cost of power, Ministry of Power is aware that for development of the economy, electricity has to be
affordable. To remain competitive in the global economy, Indian Industry needs to reduce the cost of inputs including
power. To address the issue of rising cost of power for industries etc., the Ministry of Power has adopted a two – pronged
strategy – Reduction of cost of power itself on the one hand and reduction and    elimination of cross subsidies, on the other.
The Ministry constituted an Inter-Disciplinary Group under the Chairmanship of Special Secretary (Power)  to go into the
question of reducing the cost of power.  The report of the Group is being implemented.  As regards reduction of cross
subsidies, the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998 empowers the Regulatory Commissions for the purpose. So far
13 State Electricity Regulatory Commissions have passed tariff orders, which reflect a trend towards tariff rationalization
and progressive reduction of cross subsidies.
            As regards high borrowing cost, the lending rates have gone down after the deregulation of interest rates regime. The
RBI in its mid-term review of monetary and credit policy for 2002-03 has cut the benchmark bank rate by quarter percent to
6.25 per cent and cash reserve ratio (CRR) to 4.75 per cent from 5 percent. The Commercial Banks are expected to lower
their lending rates for borrowers.  As per extant guidelines the banks are required to fix their own prime lending rates
(PLRs) and the maximum band over the PLR.  The interest rates on loans up to Rs. 2 lakh should not exceed the PLR and
that beyond Rs. 2 lakh is left to the discretion of the banks subject to PLR and the maximum bands.  The banks have been
advised to accord SSI units with a good track record the benefit of lower spreads over the PLR.
 
Further Recommendation
 
 
            The Ministry of Power has adopted a two pronged strategy – Reduction of cost of power  it self on the one hand and
reduction elimination of cross subsidies, on the other. The Committee would like to know how far reduction of the cost of
power,  tariff rationalization progressive reduction of  cross subsides  have been achieved in the state of Uttar Pradesh.
            The banks have been advised to accord SSI Units with a good track record, the benefit of lower spreads over the
PLR. The Committee would like to know how the number of SSI Units benefited by such advice given to the banks.
 
STAGNATION OF MINI CEMENT PLANTS
 
3.2
       Recommendation

            Another major constraint in this segment is excess capacity. During the growth phase of the industry, almost all
major players in this sector had gone for huge capacity addition. As a result, the installed capacity of cement industry
doubled in the last four years. In 1996-97 the installed capacity was 96.25 million tonnes, going up to 105.25 million tonnes
in 1997-98. Some additional capacity is still expected to be installed in the coming years. Due to the huge capacity available
with major plants, they have encroached upon the segment of the mini cement plants by entering the remotest areas. Mini
cement plants,which traditionally used to cater to the local markets of remote areas, were therefore badly affected.
(Para 5.2)
Action Taken
 
            The Ministry of Commerce & Industry had requested Tariff Commission (erstwhile BICP) on January 22,1999 to
undertake a study of mini cement plants and suggest measures for their revival in view of deteriorating operational
efficiency. The Tariff Commission conducted the study on all India basis and submitted a report which, however, did not
recommend granting of any further concession to the mini cement plants.
            The report concluded that after delicensing of cement industry, as part of liberalization policy in 1991, the growth of
mini-cement plants stagnated. Large cement plants, on the other hand, registered higher growth both in capacity and
production. The large cement plants being high volume and low cost producers, contributing about 95 per cent of the total
cement production in the country, are the market price leaders. Mini cement plants are the followers and vulnerable to low
sales realization. From the recommendations of the Tariff Commission it emerges that revival of these units is possible only
when they improve their operational efficiency.  
 
Further Recommendation
 
            As a result of liberalization the cement industry has been delicensed. The result was stagnation of mini cement plants
and registration of higher growth by large cement plants. As per Tariff commission recommendation, these units can be
revived when they improve their operational efficiency. Tariff Commission has not given any plan of action in this regard.
Ministry of Small Scale Industries should suggest some measures to improve their operational efficiency.
 
HIGH RATE OF INTEREST CHARGED BY UPFC
 
3.3
       Recommendation   
 
The Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation also entrusted ICRA with the job of preparing a report on the cement sector. 
The ICRA had cited high interest rate charged by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation as one of the problems faced by the
SSI units in cement sectors.
(Para 5.4)
Action Taken
 
The Banks / FIs usually determine the rate of interest to be charged on their term loans based on their cost of funds,
administrative overheads and also the risk perception of the borrower. Accordingly, the SFCs ( including UPFC) have been
retaining a margin of 3 % per annum over the rate of interest on refinance made available by IDBI and SIDBI.
With regard to the rate of interest charged by SIDBI on the refinance, it may be mentioned that the refinance rates,
as a matter of policy, are fixed below the prime lending rate (PLR) so that the cost of funds to the ultimate borrowers is
contained. With a view to mitigating the hardships of the SSI units because of the upward revision in interest rates during
early 1990s, SIDBI, in May,1995, gave an opportunity as a one time measure to SFCs including UPFC to review such cases
and claim refund of excess interest charged to certain categories of borrowers subject to the condition that similar benefit
should be passed on to their ultimate borrowers.
 
Further Recommendation
 
            It is not known whether UPFC had taken the opportunity offered by the SIDBI to review  the cases where excess
interest was charged to certain borrowers. If  UPFC had reviewed such cases. The Committee may be apprised of the
number of cases in which the benefit was passed on to their ultimate borrowers. 
 
3.4       Recommendation     
   
The Committee observes that the State Government had revised the rate of interest from 13.5% to 19.75% in 1991-
92.  The reasons for charging high rate of interest by Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation was due to the fact that it got loans

from SIDBI/ IDBI at a higher rate.  The Committee, however, feels that revising the rate of interest was not in the interest of
mini cement plants.  The Government should have calculated the viability of those projects before revising the rate of
interest as it proved a disincentive for SSIs in the cement sector.  As regards giving loan by SIDBI/ IDBI on higher rate of
interest to Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, the Committee observes that the matter should have been sorted out by the
U.P. Administration with SIDBI/ IDBI.
(Para 5.5)
 
Action Taken
 
Uttar Pradesh Financial Corporation (UPFC) gets its refinance from SIDBI/IDBI for its loan disbursals. The interest
rates of the Corporation are charged in line with refinance rates by retaining 2 or 3% as intermediation charges. UPFC has
reported that most of the cement units had been sanctioned term loans in late eighties and they did fairly well thereafter.   It
was only during 1995-96 when such units went in for major expansion, which was immediately followed by industrial
recession.  Thereafter, these units started defaulting. The interest rate charged by the Corporation were in line with the
interest rates prevailing that time in the financial sector.  At the time of working out the profitability, such units were found
viable even at this higher rate of interest.  It was only when the cement from big plants started flowing in the market, such
units started facing competition.  The small scale units could not raise their sale price in consonance with rise in input cost
because of constraints of the market.  Most of the financial institutions do not revise their interest rate during the currency of
loan.  The interest rates are fixed and are the same which are prevailing at the time of first disbursement.  Thus it would not
have been possible for the Corporation to lower the interest rates even if these units started defaulting.
 
Further Recommendation
 
            From the Ministry’s comments the sordid tale of mini cement plants in Uttar Pradesh has come to the fore. These
plants cannot be held responsible as they have become victims due to delicensing  of cement industry. The Committee
suggests that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries should mediate between the UPFC and SIDBI to find a suitable solution
like one time settlement.
 
WAIVING OF INTEREST BY UPFC
 
3.5       Recommendation  
 
The Committee notes that SSIs engaged in this business took loans from the financial institutions/ banks, but due to
industrial slow down  and stiff competition from giant plants they had to dispose of their products through distress sale,
which contributed to accumulation of interest against the principal amount of loan.  Raising of interest by Government
under such circumstances proved to be the death knell for the SSIs in the cement sector.  The Committee further notes that
Rajasthan Financial Corporation, under a one time settlement, not only waived the interest completely but also waived 20%
principal amount so that the mini cement units situated in Rajasthan may survive.
(Para 5.6)
 
Action Taken
 
The UPFC has stated that they are not aware of any such scheme of waiver of interest completely and also waiver of
20% of principal amount of the mini cement plants in Rajsthan.  The Corporation would be writing to RFC to find out the
details about this scheme.
The Board of U.P. Financial Corporation had decided to charge only 12% simple interest on the outstanding loan
amount from the date of first default, while deciding the OTS of these cases.  Further, the amount paid by the units during
the interregnum would also be deducted from the OTS amount.  Further, the Corporation has approved some of the OTS
cases even by charging 7-8% simple interest on outstanding principal amount from the date of first default.  This has been
done keeping in view the paying capacity of the borrower.  Thus, the Corporation has been quite sympathetic to the
problems of sick cement units.
 
 
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee wonders what prevented Ministry of Small Scale Industries to find out from  RFC about the scheme

and explore the possibility whether it cannot be followed in toto in Uttar Pradesh. The Committee takes strong exception to
the fact that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries has left it to UPFR to find out from RFC if there was any scheme of
waiving from SSI units in Rajasthan.
 
3.6       Recommendation    
 
The units of Uttar Pradesh are working in a climate of apathy.  Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, in a letter dated
October 4,2000 addressed to “Udyog Bandhu” (A Forum of Industrial Associations), mentioned that the members of the
mini cement plants association desired that whatever repayment (by way of interest or repayment) they have made till date
to the Corporation may be adjusted towards principal and balance may be recovered from them in easy installments. The
Board had already rejected this proposal earlier. However, if there is any demand of the association for waiver of total or
part of interest, the same is to be taken to the Board again for its approval.
(Para 5.7)
Action Taken
 
The UPFC has stated that keeping in view large scale recession prevailing in cement sector, the Corporation has
been quite sympathetic to the problems of mini cement units. The amount paid by the cement units by way of interest or
principal has been adjusted towards total OTS amount which has been arrived after adding 7% to 12% simple interest from
the date of first default on the principal outstanding. As rightly mentioned UPFC Board has rejected the proposal of OTS on
principal outstanding only. As regards the waiver of part of interest is concerned the same is acceptable to the Corporation.
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee still feels that the decision taken by R.F.C can be followed in the SSI Sector in Uttar Pradesh also.
The Committee therefore recommends that the UPFC may explore the possibility of taking similar decision as taken by
R.F.C, Rajasthan.
3.7
       Recommendation     
 
The Committee fails to understand as to why Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation is not able to bail out the units in
UP taking a cue from the RFC when the units in UP are struggling for survival.
(Para 5.8)
 
Action Taken
 
UPFC has stated that they are not aware of the scheme of RFC. They would be writing to RFC to find out the details
of the scheme.
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee hopes that the details of the scheme would be found by UPFC and  implemented without
delay.
 
INTER DEPARTMENTAL COORDINATION TO HELP SSI UNITS
 
3.8       Recommendation     
 
From the memorandum submitted by the Association, the Committee notes that problems of the units were to be
deliberated by a High Power Committee under the Chairmanship of the Chief Minister. In this regard, the Directorate of
Industries, UP, in their letter dated August 1
st ,2000 requested Secretary, UP Administration, to place the matter before the
said High Power Committee. It appears that such a sensitive matter was not brought before that Committee.  It reflects lack
of coordination between the departments of the Government.  Similar situations also prevail at the central level also.  On
various occasions, the Committee observed that various Ministries did not have an integrated approach to solve the
problems of the industry.  The Committee observes that if SSI units are to be given a boost, the different departments of the
State Government and Central Government are to work in a coordinated manner.
(Para 5.9)
 
Action Taken

The Directorate of Industries, U.P. has stated that U.P. Mini Cement Plants Association submitted a letter on the
problems of mini cement industries to the Directorate in the year 2000 which was sent to the U.P. Government to place
before the High Power Committee of Udyog Bandhu under the Chairmanship of the Hon’ble Chief Minister. However, due
to some unavoidable circumstances the proposed meeting on October 21 st ,.2000 could not be held.  Meanwhile, a letter
from the Association on the issues concerning the same subject matter was received which has been referred vide letter
dated October 4th ,2002 with recommendations of the Directorate for consideration at the State Government level. The main
problems raised by the Association relate to facilities desired from the UPFC. The Corporation has apprised regarding the
present status on the action/ steps taken in the matter.  Thus, U.P. Financial Corporation and the State Government are
serious about taking positive action.
The State Level Inter-Institutional Committee (SLIICs) have been set up in all the States under the Chairmanship of
Secretary, Industries Department of the concerned State to deal with the problems of coordination for rehabilitation of sick
SSI units.
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee is happy to note that UPFC and State Governments are serious about taking positive action. The
Committee would like to know the follow up action taken in the matter.
 
TECHNOLOGY USED IN MINI CEMENT PLANTS
 
3.9
       Recommendation   
 
            The Central Government had facilitated in establishing the mini cement plants to meet the demand of cement in the
emerging scenario of building up of infrastructure facilities in the country by enabling the SSI sector to get loans from the
IDBI.  In all, 126 units were set up, of which 50% were in the category of integrated units (which produced cement out of its
own manufactured clinkers) and 50% were in the category of grindingunits (which ground clinkers to produce cement after
purchasing clinkers from the big units).  This method of producing cement by the SSI sector received a setback when the
Supreme Court banned mining of limestone and as a consequence, limestone mines were closed in Dehradun.   As a result,
thesupply of major raw material i.e. limestone, had stopped and self-producing capacity of units for making clinker
vanished.  The remaining units are doing only grinding by purchasing clinker from the big units.  The woes of SSI sector
did not end here.  The capacity to produce clinker and producing cement out of clinker has not only been taken away by the
big units from the SSI sector, the price of clinker sold by them to small units has been raised to such an extent that either the
small units are unable to purchase it from big units or if they purchase and grind them, they would not be able to sell that
cement in the market because of high cost of production, resulting in closure of mini cement plants.
(Para 5.13)
 
Action Taken
 
The manufacture of cement in the composite units is made by calcining the typical  composition either in a vertical
shaft kiln or rotary kiln.  The environmental factors or other problems like dependence on large units for clinkers,
inadequacies in infrastructure,   rise in input costs etc. coupled with lower sales realization have affected the mini cement
plants.  As revealed by the study conducted by the Tariff Commission among the rotary kiln plants, plants which have
upgraded their capacity have improved their productivity and energy efficiency which had a favourable impact on their cost
of production as well as profitability.  Vertical shaft kiln plants were affected more severely than rotary kiln plants. 
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee feels that by improving the technology, the mini cement plants still may be made viable. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries may lend a helping hand to SSI Sector in this
regard.
 
INCENTIVES TO LARGE CEMENT PLANTS
 
3.10     Recommendation          
 
Recently, the UP Government had offered 100% concession of Sales tax for 12 years to those industries whose

115th report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/115threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:26:02]
investment is over PSUs crore.  Under this scheme, the giant cement industries like ACC and Satna Cement have
established their grinding unit of total 8.6 lakh tonnes per annum capacity in Rai Bareily District of UP  and are availing of
this concession.  The State Government would lose a huge amount of revenue by granting this concession to the giant units. 
The cement so produced after grinding by the giant units is much cheaper and their selling price is much lower than that of
mini plants.  All the more, the giant units are availing double concessions: -
(a)
    Firstly, as a manufacturer of intermediate product i.e. clinker, they are availing sales tax exemption in their parent
State; and
(b)   they are availing sales tax concession in UP as a manufacturer of cement.
(Para 5.14)
 
Action Taken
 
            While cement (large/small) units set up in backward areas are eligible for sales tax benefits, small scale units enjoy
excise duty benefits.  The issue of availability of sales tax/ other benefits to cement units (either large or small) is a State
subject and will have to be addressed by the State Government. 
            Ministry of Finance has informed that in the Conference of Chief Ministers of States/ UTs held on 16
th November,
1999, it was decided sales tax based incentive schemes must be withdrawn by all the State Governments.  Accordingly,
most of the State Governments have withdrawn sales tax based incentives given to industries, except the pipeline cases.
 
 
Further Recommendation
 
            Although sales Tax is a state subject the Committee desires that Ministry of Small Scale Industries should obtain the
information from the State Government for information of the Committee.
 
3.11
     Recommendation  
 
            During the course of oral evidence before the Sub-Committee, the SSI association expressed the apprehension that
those giant industries would leave UP after 12 years and establish their units in other States to avail sale tax concession. 
The Committee was informed that small units are given only two years sales tax free concession as against 12 years to the
giant units.
(Para 5.15)
Action Taken
 
Same as given under para 5.14.  In view of the position stated, the apprehension that giant industries would leave the
State and establish their units elsewhere to avail  sales tax concession is unfounded. 
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee would like to know whether any large Company has left the State after availing concession
for twelve years.
 
3.12     Recommendation    
            Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation’s letter dated 4 th October 2000 addressed to “Udyog Bandhu” corroborates the
above fact.  The study made by ICRA had concluded that integrated mini cement units were not viable.  The report further
concluded that in case the unit took up grinding function alone, the operation could become viable with some incentives. 
The study had further concluded that the units could be marginally viable if they were granted total sales tax exemption.  It
has been further mentioned that Government of UP had granted 12 years sales tax exemption to big units.  The revenue loss
to Government from these two units alone would be Rs. 345 crores.  It had been reported that there was a third new large
unit coming up in the State.  Revenue loss from this unit alone would be Rs. 691 crores.
(Para 5.16)
 
Action Taken
 
            The only concession  that is at present available to mini cement plants is in the nature of reduced excise duty to those
mini cement plants which produce cement up to 99,000 MT per annum. So far as concessions to mini cement units for the
revival of these units in the State of Uttar Pradesh by way of preference treatment for their product, waiver of sales tax, etc.

is concerned, the matter concerns the State Government.
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee desires that the information may be obtained from the State Government for information of the
Committee.
 
PURCHASE PREFERENCE POLICY
 
3.13     
Recommendation   
 
            The above communication is the testimony of the fact how small units are discriminated against and have been
forced to wage a battle against stronger competitors.
When the small units were gasping for oxygen, UP government issued a circular in 1998 asking its cement
consuming departments to send their demands to small-scale industries only.  In spite of this, Government departments are
not complying with the order.  As a result, the order remained on paper only without any visible results.  The Committee
feels that a mechanism to monitor the compliance of the Purchase Preference Policy should have been evolved if the
Government really wanted to help the SSI sector.   The  Committee  observes that an early action
 
 
to monitor the compliance of the order even now may save the situation for the dying SSI units.
(Para 5.17)
Action Taken
 
The issue of preferential treatment to small- scale cement units for their product  pertains to the U.P. Government.
There already exists a Government Purchase & Price Preference Policy wherein certain facilities/ benefits are being
provided to the SSI units as a marketing support measure. The Draft “Small Enterprises Development Bill” under 
consideration of the Ministry of SSI  also covers the aspect of measures for trade protection.
 
Further Recommendation
 
The Committee desires that Ministry of Small Scale Industries may obtain information from the State Government
about the extent to which Purchase and Price Preference Policy is implemented for the benefit of mini cement plants.
 
CREDIT FLOW TO MINI CEMENT PLANTS
 
3.14     
Recommendation   
 
Another factor which has crippled the mini cement plants is the lack of credit flow to the sector. While the giant
units had no difficulty in securing loans from banks and FIs, the small units are still struggling to get loans from banks even
after the announcement made to the effect that loan would be given without any collateral security. In addition, restriction
on load carrying capacity of trucks proved to be a strangulatory provision for the mini cement plants.
(Para 5.18)
 
Action Taken
 
 The RBI has advised the banks in January, 2002 to extend the benefit under the increased exemption limit of 
borrowal accounts for obtention of collateral securities of Rs. 5 lakh to all SSI units  so as to ensure flow of credit to this
sector.  Further, the RBI in April, 2002 has advised the banks that they may, on the basis of good track record and financial
position of the units, increase the limit of dispensation of collateral requirement for loans from the existing Rs. 5 lakh to Rs.
15 lakh. 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
The Committee would like to know the extent of credit flown to mini cement plants under the R.B.I.
guidelines.

ECONOMIC RECESSION AND SLOW DOWN IN THE ECONOMY
 
3.15     Recommendation   
 
In nutshell, a vision was created during the successive Five Year Plans and notifications issued in 1979 that huge
infrastructure would be created nationwide but large cement plants would not be in a position to supply the required
quantum of cement. SSI sector was encouraged to set up mini cement plants to meet the demand of additional quantum of
cement in view of its lower capital cost, quicker installation and higher employment potential coupled with the exploitation
of smaller limestone deposits by it in rural and hilly areas. These units were given loan assistance by the banks and FIs and
they started setting up units when the cement industry was hailed as the harbinger of overall development of the state. The
good days for the SSI sector did not last long due to economic recession when construction activities come to a low ebb.
(Para 6.1)
 
Action Taken
 
            Following the decontrol   of Indian Cement Industry   there   had  been   large-scale   capacity   expansion  and 
growth   in  cement production in the country, particularly,  in the 90’s.  However, upsurge in demand for cement was not as
expected due to general recession and slowdown in the economy affecting the industrial growth.  Large cement plants in the
vicinity of mini cement plants tend to charge lower prices which have further eroded the profitability of the mini cement
plants.  Rise in input costs coupled with lower sales realization further affected profitability.  Vertical shaft kiln plants were
affected more severely than rotary kiln plants. 
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Comments of the Ministry of the Small Scale Industries reveal the stark reality. Vertical shaft kiln plants have
no future but rotary kiln plants can survive the situation with upgraded capacity. Now the question before the Government
whether uneconomic plants may be given decent burial or they may be given technological advice to upgrade their capacity.
The Committee recommends that an all out effort may be made by the Government to the help the mini cement plants.
 
 
PROBABILITY OF MINI CEMENT PLANTS TO REPAY LOAN
 
3.16     
Recommendation   
 
            SSI’s cup of sorrow was full when the Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation increased the rate of interest from 13.5%
to 19.75% per cent and the giant units flooded the market with their brand of cement at a much lower price than that of mini
cement plants which in turn were forced them to sell cement at a price lower than their cost of production. They failed to
pay interest on the principal amount and the banks and FIs shut their doors to these sick units.
(Para 6.2)
Action Taken
 
SIDBI has opined that the rate of interest in term loan is determined usually at the time of disbursement and does not
vary during the entire period of the loan.  Such of those cases of potentially viable sick SSI units could be covered under
SIDBI’s Refinance Scheme for Rehabilitation of sick SSI units subject to the proposals meeting the norms and parameters
of the scheme.  Under the scheme, it was possible to consider reduction of interest rate, if so warranted. 
 
 
Further Recommendation
 
            The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries may make an effort to bring the SSI units
under the ambit of SIDBI’s scheme for Rehabilitation of sick  SSI units.
 
IMPLEMENTATION OF ICRA REPORT ON MINI CEMENT PLANTS
3.17      Recommendation    
 
Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation made a study about problems and possible revival scheme of mini cement plants

through ICRA, which suggested complete waiver of interest coupled with full exemption of sales tax and imposition of 15%
price preference for the revival of mini cement plants. But so far, no positive step has been taken to save the industry.
(Para 6.3)
Action Taken
 
UPFC has stated that M/s ICRA had arrived at this conclusion about three years back. The ground situation during
this time has changed significantly. It would need fresh calculation to find out as to whether these sick units would be viable
in case they are given total interest waiver coupled with full exemption of sales tax and imposition of 15% price preference.
 
Further Recommendation
 
It is clear that no action was taken to implement ICRA report. It remains on paper only. Had it been implemented the
plight of SSI units would have been different.  The Ministry in their own comment admitted that there was need to have
fresh calculation about the viability of the sick units. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take a fresh
initiative in this regard.
 
RECENT DEMAND FOR CEMENT
 
3.18     Recommendation  
 
The Committee observes that in the recent past, there has been an overall increase in the rate of growth in the cement
industry.  This is an indication that construction activity has again picked up.  But these activities are confined to certain
places in the country and, by and large, large industries are able to reap the benefit of such a situation.  The renewed demand
for cement has not percolated to the lower level of the industry.  The Committee feels a lending hand should be given to
those sick units.  Ways and means should be explored to bail out them from then pathetic situation.
(Para 6.4)
Action Taken
 
Ministry of Commerce & Industry, Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion has stated that cement is now fully
decontrolled industry and no licence is required from that department for setting up of cement plant in any part of the
country either in large or small scale sector. Further, the Central Government does not provide any incentives for setting up
a small scale unit in the cement sector. The only concession that is at present given to mini cement plants is in the nature of
reduced excise duty which is granted to those mini cement plants which produce cement up to 99,000 MT per annum. As
mentioned earlier, the Ministry of Commerce & Industry had requested Tariff Commission (erstwhile BICP) to undertake a
study of mini cement plants and suggest measures for their revival. The Tariff Commission in its report did not recommend
granting of any further concession to the mini cement plants.
            The cases of potentially viable sick SSI units could, however, be considered under SIDBI’s Refinance Scheme for
Rehabilitation of sick SSI units subject to the proposals meeting the norms and parameters of the scheme. 
 
 
 
Further Recommendation
 
            From the reply given by the Ministry of SSI it is clear that revival of mini cement plants in Uttar Pradesh mainly
depends on the State Government and SIDBI. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should impress upon the State
Government and SIDBI to come out with some measures to help the industry.

3.19     Recommendation  
 
In view of the RBI guidelines, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Small Scale Industries, in consultation
with the RBI, Lead Bank, Uttar Pradesh Finance Corporation, and UP Administration should make an attempt to revive
these units keeping in view the ICRA report as well as action initiated by the Rajasthan Financial Corporation so that these
units, which are more or less victims of circumstances, can survive.
(Para 6.6)

As regards, mechanism to assess the sickness of SSIs and revival route for sick SSIs, the RBI has issued on 16 th
January,2002  revised, detailed, transparent and non-discretionary guidelines based on Kohli Committee recommendations

REPORT
 
            The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises) on the recommendations contained in the 82 nd Report of the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on MoU
System in Strategic Sector PSEs, which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 10th December, 2002.
 
            Action Taken Notes have been received from the Department of Public Enterprises in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report.
They have been categorized as follows:-
 
i)
                    Recommendations/Observations which will be conveyed to the concerned PSE and the Administrative Ministry for appropriate action.
(Chapter-I). Para nos.:   4.18.1, 4.18.2, 4.18.4, 6.13.2, 6.13.5, 6.13.10, 5.8.7, 5.8.8.
 
ii)
                  Recommendations/Observations which will be conveyed to the Administrative ministry to include suitable parameter in MoU in the next
year or will be kept in View before finalizing next year’s MoU. (Chapter-II). Para nos.:4.18.3, 5.8.1, 5.8.2, 5.8.5, 6.13.4, 6.13.8, 6.13.9.
 
iii)                 Recommendations/Observations which have been noted by the Department. (Chapter-III). Paras nos.4.18.5, 4.18.6, 5.8.4, 5.8.6, 6.13.3,
6.13.6, 6.13.7.
 
iv)                Recommendations/Observation on which Department have not prepared any action. Para nos. 5.8.3
 
The details of the ATR are reproduced in various chapters in the succeeding pages.

BHARAT EARTH MOVERS LIMITED
 
 
1.1            OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee was pleased to note that BEML had been showing profits since its inception. However, the Committee was concerned to note that
there has been a constant decline in the profits over the past several years. The Committee feels that BEML has not made adequate efforts to expand its
market base. The Committee recommends that BEML should resort to aggressive marketing and explore new areas beyond their traditional customers to
expand their market base. In this context the Committee feels that BEML should develop value added products so as to garner a larger share of the market.
The Committee is of the view that with the infrastructure sector looking up, there are tremendous opportunities for BEML. The Committee also feels that
BEML should also explore the possibilities of providing maintenance service for high cost machines.
 
(para no. 4.18.1)
Reply of the Government
 
The recommendations of the Committee will be conveyed to the PSE as well as the Administrative Ministry for taking appropriate action with the
advice to formulate appropriate strategy.
 
 
1.2            OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee was deeply concerned to note that BEML has not been able to get adequate work orders for its railway coach-manufacturing unit at
Bangalore. The Committee is of the opinion that BEML should approach organizations like the Delhi Metro Corporation to obtain work orders, and the
issue should be taken up with the Railway authorities at the highest level.
(para no. 4.18.2)
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
The recommendation of the Committee will be communicated to the PSE and the Railway Board for taking immediate appropriate action. 
 
1.3            OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee felt that since the MOU is a mutually agreed document on performance parameters, a focus shift in the contribution of Government
for this type of PSE is also imperative.  The performance parameters of the Department of Defence Production and Supply in the MOU should lay
emphasis on more tangible factors like facilitating more orders from Railways for their products, export promotion for their remote controlled armoured
vehicles, extension of use of export offices of other PSUs like Bharat Electronics etc in other countries for promotion of BEML products etc.
 
(para no. 4.18.4)
 
Reply of the Government
 
While in the emerging economic environment obtaining orders is primarily a managerial function, however, the Administrative Ministry can
always play a more pro-active role in this regard.  The recommendation of the Committee relating to promotion of exports from the PSE will be brought to
the notice of the Administrative Ministry with the request to support the efforts of the PSE in promotion of its exports.
