HINDUSTAN AERONAUTICS LIMITED
 
2.2            OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee was pleased to note that HAL had been showing profits since its inception. In addition, the Committee felt that HAL needs to make
adequate efforts to expand its market base as well as its product and services base. In this context, the Committee asked the management to outline the
vision of the HAL over a 20-year period. The Committee recommends that HAL should resort to diversifying  its market base into aviation sector of State
Governments, Agro Aviation, remote sensing etc. and also should expand to new products and services instead of present dispensation of excessive
dependence on the Indian Air force. In this context the Committee feels that HAL should develop testing and servicing facilities, drawings and design
consultancies etc.  so as to ensure their  presence in  a larger arena in the market especially with better coordination with Ministry of Civil Aviation, State
Governments, Ministry of Agriculture, Disaster Relief Agencies etc.
(para no. 5.8.1)
 
Reply of the Government
 
The recommendation of the Committee will be brought to the notice of the PSE as well as the Administrative Ministry.  This Department has
already issued guidelines to all the PSEs to include strategic issues in their MOUs.  In view of the recommendation of the Committee the PSE will be
requested to prepare its strategic plan by incorporating their strategy of marketing and diversification.
 
 
2.3            OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee also observed that having regard to the vital sector in which the unit is operating,  the structure of the MOU should be more
appropriately geared to this factor.  It was observed that the focus on financial performance being reiterated in the MOU should be altered to shift the focus
on more important factors of national interest. Hence the MOU should accord higher weightage to performance parameters relating to R&D, contribution
to defence, contribution to Indian Space Research Programme, Disaster Management and Relief efforts etc.
(para no. 5.8.2)
 
 
Reply of the Government
 
In case of HAL the financial parameters are accorded the weightage of 40%, which was 60% earlier.  The main objective of giving higher
weightage to the financial parameter is to ensure the financial viability of the PSEs so that this crucial aspect, which is essential for their existence, is not
lost sight of. The recommendation of the Committee is noted and efforts will be made to accord comparatively higher weightage to the parameters relating
to R&D, Contribution to Defence, Disaster Management and Relief Efforts, etc.
 
 
 
2.4            OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee also felt that since the unit is operating in a strategic sector it is imperative that it has a sound policy for retention and upgradation
of skills of its Human Resource.  This is more than imperative for a unit like HAL having regard to its strategic contribution to India’s defence and
infrastructure sector. It is therefore felt that the weightage for HRD should also be higher.
(para no.  5.8.5)
Reply of the Government
 
 
The recommendation of the Committee will be kept in view while finalizing the MOU for the next year.

CHAPTER –  IV
HINDUSTAN AERONAUTICS LIMITED
 
4.1            OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee felt that since the MOU is a mutually agreed document on performance parameters, a focus shift in the contribution of Government
for this type of PSU is also imperative.  The performance parameters of the Department of Defence Production and Supply in the MOU should emphasis
on more tangible factors like facilitating more orders from non Defence areas for their products, export promotion activities for their products, extension of
use of export offices of other PSUs like BharatElectronics etc in other countries for promotion of HAL products and services etc. In addition it was also
felt by the Committee that Government should also extend its assistance in ensuring HAL’s participation in UN Projects, including sale of its helicopters
for UN Peace Keeping Missions, UN activities in other relief and rehabilitation programmes in war torn, disasteraffected areas.  The Government should
also enable HAL in ensuring their participation in such activities of other multilateral agencies. In addition, during a demonstration of Helicopter testing
the Committee appreciated the testing competence of the HAL.  The Committee felt that these facilities and competencies are of international standards
and the government should strive hard to enable the export of these facilities and services to other countries.
(para no. 5.8.3)
 
Reply of the Government
 
It is true that MOU is a mutually agreed document and ideally the responsibilities of  both the parties should be clearly indicated in document itself.
While finalizing the MOU targets during the MOU negotiation meetings the managements of the PSEs are required to clearly indicate the assistance
required from the Government to achieve those targets.  In fact, there is a separate section in the MOU which clearly specifies the responsibility of the
Government in order to achieve the set targets and the evaluation of the performance of the PSE at the end of the year is carried out by taking into account
the extent of fulfillment of obligations on the part of the Government.  In case, the Government fail to fulfill these obligations the management of the PSE
is not allowed to suffer on account of it. Otherwise also, in the changing economic environment it is the role of the management to strengthen the
operations of the PSE and the Administrative Ministry of course, can play a more pro-active role to ensure the growth the PSE on a long-term basis.

  INTRODUCTION
          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred-Seventeenth Report on the Demands for Grants (2003-04)
pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries.
2.       The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry heard the representatives of Small Scale
Industries Associations on the subject on 26th March, 2003 and the Secretary, Ministry of Small Scale Industries on
27th March, 2003.
3.       The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the Draft report
at its meeting held on 6th May 2003.
NEW DELHI;
6 May, 2003
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
1.1     The Ministry of Small Scale Industries is the nodal Ministry for policy formulation, promotion, development and
protection of Small Scale Industries. It also monitors the implementation of these policies.
1.2     Ministry of SSI designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and growth of
small enterprises. The Ministry also coordinates with other Ministries/Departments on behalf of the Small Scale
Industries (SSI) sector.
1.3     Implementation of policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services to
small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organization
(SIDO).
1.4     The Indian economy has experienced profound changes and sustained growth in the last five decades. Industry
sector, by building core strength of the economy, has acted as an engine of growth. The Small Scale Industries (SSI)
sector has also contributed significantly in process of growth and has emerged as a vibrant partner. The importance of
the sector can be well assessed in terms of its contribution to the socio-economic objectives of growth in generation of
employment, output, exports.
1.5     The SSI sector, producing a wide range of products, accounts for around 95 per cent of the industrial units in the
country, contributing to 40 per cent of the manufacturing sector output and approximately one-third of the Nation's
exports. As at end-March, 2002, there were 34.42 lakh SSI units providing direct employment to around 192.33 lakh
persons. As per the estimates of the office of the Development Commissioner (SSI), the output of SSI sector at current
prices aggregated Rs. 6,90,316 crores during the year 2001-02 and exports at the level of Rs. 69.797 crores during the
2000-01. During the financial year 2002-03, the production of SSI sector at current prices is projected to reach at Rs. 7,
42,021 crores. The sector also acts as a nursery for promoting entrepreneurial talents and as a catalyst in the industrial
growth.
1.6     There has been a structural relationship between the SSI sector's growth and the growth of industry and the
overall economy. The comparative annual growth rates of the overall industry, manufacturing and SSI sectors show that
the small scale industry sector has been generally recording a rate of growth higher than that overall industry and
manufacturing sectors growth rates. During the financial year 2001-02, the SSI sector achieved a growth of 6.08 per
cent in comparison with a 3.3 per cent growth recorded by the overall industry sector and 3.4 per cent by the
manufacturing sector.

117th Report of Committee on Industry

1.7     The SSI sector has been receiving due attention from the Government as well as other extension agencies through
various policies by way of financial and fiscal incentives, infrastructural facilities, technology, marketing and other
similar support measures. For credit dispensation, SSI sector has been accorded status of "priority sector" by banks.
However, with the onset of economic reforms and globalisation, a number of challenges and opportunities have
emerged for the sector. While, on the one hand, the process of liberalization has expanded the scope of cross-border
transactions, on the other, the new order has led to different perceptions about the protection and safeguards that the SSI
sector has hitherto enjoyed. The changed environment has necessitated technology upgradation, quality standardization
and strengthening of marketing facilities for various products, more particularly, the SSI products, to tap the expanded
horizons.
1.8     The process of liberalization and market reforms has created wide-ranging opportunities for the development of
small-scale industries. At the same time, changing world scenario has thrown up new challenges to the very existence of
the sector. Moreover, this sector has also been facing some problems related to credit, infrastructure, technology,
marketing, delayed payments, problems on account of complex rules and regulation etc. The need of the hour is to
suitably strengthen the sector so that it can adapt itself to the changed environment and face challenges boldly and
effectively. In order to enable this sector to avail the opportunities and play its role as an engine of growth, the Hon'ble
Prime Minister on 30th August, 2000 announced a Comprehensive Policy Package for the SSI Sector.
1.9     The small enterprises have emerged as a focus area for forging and promoting trade. Economic reform
programmes envisage the emergence of Indian Industry as a global competitor with substantial presence in the
international markets. Technology upgradation and modernization of SSI sector and promotion of export from this
sector are interlinked issues, which are important objectives behind promoting international cooperation. Nine countries
viz.; USA, Germany, Italy, South Korea, U.K., Taiwan, Japan, Singapore and Israel have been identified as the thrust
countries for promoting enterprise-to-enterprise cooperation to upgrade the capabilities of Indian SSI sector to make it
competitive in the global markets. This has assumed greater significance in the context of the liberalization process. In
fact, the potential of SSI sector for contributing to exports and creating employment remains untapped in the absence of
access to technology and other factors.

3.3     The Office of the Development Commissioner (Small Scale Industries) headed by the Development
Commissioner is an attached office of the Ministry for formulating, coordinating and monitoring policies and
programmes for promotion and development of small-scale industries in the country. It maintains close liaison with
Central Ministries, Planning Commission, State Governments, Financial Institutions, Voluntary Organisations and other

Secretaries of the various Departments, Financial Institutions, Public Sector Undertakings and representatives from
Parliament, Industry Associations and eminent experts in the field.
3.5     The Committee observes that in the era of globalisation and liberalisation of the economy, the Small Scale
Industries should be strengthened to compete in the international markets. Policy measures should be formulated and
relevant data should be obtained through surveys, investigations and studies. The Committee recommends that the role
of Development Commissioner for SSI should be oriented in accordance with the ever-changing scenario so as to make
the SSI sector internationally competitive.
3.6     The Committee further observes that it has become extremely essential to create awareness about India's
obligations under the WTO regime and their impact on various sectors. Having heard the representatives of Powerloom,
Readymade garment, Pan Masala Associations, the Committee draws an inference that there is some communication
gap between the SIDO and SSI Associations. Therefore the Committee recommends that there should be regular
interaction between the Government and Small Scale Industries. A Committee at local level should also be formed
between Bankers and local chapters of SSI Associations to sort out their problems relating to credit related issues at
local level in all the States. The local committee should give quarterly report to the Ministry of Small Scale Industries,
Ministry of Finance (Banking Division) and Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.

VI.     CREDIT TO SSI SECTOR
6.1     The Committee is of the opinion that one of the major problems of SSIs is that of finance, whether it is equity,
term loan or working capital. Financial institutions and commercial banks are often reluctant to lend to small scale
enterprises because of the high risks involved. Moreover, the commercial banks and financial institutions that provide
working capital and term finance to the corporate borrower generally demand personal guarantees from borrowers,
besides the collateral security. This adversely affects the borrowing capacity of the small entrepreneur. The lack of
coordination between commercial banks and financial institutions causes delay in availability of working capital and
hence in the commissioning of projects. The complex and time-consuming procedures and formalities of the
institutional lenders cause operational impediments for SSI units.
6.2     The Ministry apprised the Committee that the total advances to SSI from the Public Sector Banks has gone up in
absolute terms from Rs. 48,445 crores in March, 2001 to Rs. 49,743 crores in March, 2002. The percentage of SSI
advances to Net Bank Credit (NBC) however, has declined from 14.2% as at the end of March, 2001 to 12.5% as at the
end of March, 2002. The RBI's study of the specialized SSI/general branches has revealed that adequate credit is being
made available to all viable and bankable projects.

VII.    Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries

VIII.   VENTURE CAPITAL FUND
8.1     The Committee is of the opinion that in order to encourage new entrepreneurs to set up small scale units, it is very
important to create Venture Capital facilities. With a view to meeting the needs of emerging areas and to help the small
scale units in Software/Information Technology Sector, SIDBI has taken an initiative in the launching of the
State/Regional Level Venture Capital Fund with participation from State Governments. However, Venture Capital is not
easily available to very small and tiny units. The Committee was informed that EXIM Bank has also made an entry into
venture capital finance by investing a Venture Capital Fund - India Technology Venture Unit Scheme - promoted by
Unit Trust of India.
8.2     In order to extend assistance for high risk and innovative ventures; SIDBI has started a 3-tier Venture Capital
Fund (VCF) structure for software and IT industry at the regional, national and international levels. So far, the Bank has
contributed in setting up of 15 regional and State level venture funds. Most of the funds supported by the Bank have
focus/orientation on the IT sector, though the funds are now diversifying into other knowledge based sectors in a
gradual manner. As on September 30, 2002, SIDBI has committed contribution of Rs. 121.25 crore to these funds, out
of which Rs. 69.16 crore had been disbursed. Collectively, the funds have been invested in 107 ventures by end-
September, 2002, with aggregate assistance of Rs. 270.14 crore. Out of the total assistance, 72 per cent by number and
44 per cent by amount has been extended to SSI units. In addition to State level VCFs, a National Venture Fund for
Software and IT Industry (NFSIT) has been set up at the national level in association with the Government of India,
Ministry of Information and Technology and Industrial Development Bank of India. NSFIT has a committed corpus of
Rs. 100 crore; of which an amount of Rs. 66.67 crore has been raised from the contributors upto September 30, 2002.
The cumulative sanctions by end-September, 2002, aggregated Rs. 44.84 crore. At the international level, the Bank has
entered into Memorandum of Understanding with Small Enterprise Assistance Funds (SEAF) of USA to set up SEAF
India Equity Fund and other developmental initiatives for SSIs/women entrepreneurs.
8.3     The Committee recommends that more Venture funds should be set up for information technology, biotechnology
and food processing. The Committee feels that Venture Capital could be a successful concept in bringing out the latent
entrepreneurship spirit of the youth of the country. In this context the Committee recommends that a suitable policy
framework may be designed expeditiously to promote setting up of such funds in the public as well as the private sector.
Banks should be encouraged to entertain Venture Capital funding to SSI units.

XI.     VALUE ADDED TAX  (VAT)
11.1   Value Added Tax (VAT) has emerged as one of the most important fiscal innovation of the present century with
more than 115 countries opting it. Since the setting up of "Indirect Taxation Enquiry Committee" in 1976 under
Chairmanship of Shri L.K. Jha, the Central Government has been perusing the idea of VAT. With announcing its "long
term fiscal policy" in December 1985, the Government of India moved towards implementing the modified version of
VAT for manufacturing i.e. Modified Value Added Tax (MODVAT) in 1986 and later extending its scope under
CENVAT at federal level. The Central Government facilitated the formation of Empowered Committee of States
Finance Ministers for formulation of VAT in States. After a series of meetings and development, the State VAT 
was proposed to be introduced on 1st April 2003, and over 15 States have already accepted the implementation of VAT.
11.2   The Finance Minister in his speech on Finance Bill, 2003 on 30th April, 2003 stated that VAT was a modern, a
forward looking, and a path breaking reform that the States amongst themselves actually agreed to implement. There
could not be departures from the agreed list of commodities which would be subjected to 12 and a half percent rate of
Value Added Tax. The Empowered Committee had considered these issues. It was very important that the legislation of
the States were amended to conform to the decisions taken by the Committee itself and also to the agreed upon rates
latest by 5th of May. Otherwise, it would not be possible to introduce VAT by 1st of June as suggested by the States
themselves. Government had also, therefore, to take on board the question of adequate preparations in the administrative
machinery before introduction of this very important tax reform.
          The Empowered Committee had fixed some criteria and concerned officials had got full training. The
Government had said that it would try to produce a checklist right from the Centre upto district level. It has also been
stated that it was for the States to deliberate upon the apprehensions of the traders' organizations and industrialists.
11.3   The Committee however, feels that the Central Government should establish a nodal agency, keeping in view the
interest of SSIs in particular and industry in general, in Ministry of Finance (preferably headed by an officer not below
the rank of Addl. Secretary) to coordinate implementation of VAT in States. There is a need to list the operative
problems in inter-State transactions, which could only be solved with the intervention of the Central Government.
11.4   The Committee further observes that the Central Government should act swiftly and decisively to bring in the
homogeneity in the States' VAT Acts: homogeneity in basic principles and classification.
11.5   The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance should develop an extensive information base in
Ministry's web site on VAT (or a separate site altogether to solve confusion arising out of lack of updated information at
one point.
XII.    ANTI -DUMPING MEASURES
12.1   There is expected to be large scale dumping of different products and flow of cheaper imports to Indian markets.
Imported consumer goods being of international standards in quality and competitive in prices are likely to change the
tastes of Indian consumers. It may prove to be a major factor in shrinking demand for local products. SSIs are struggling
to restructure themselves, diversify production, adopt higher standards, and have collaborations for product designs or
brands or upgraded technology for their existence. There is ignorance among Small Scale entrepreneurs about
implications of WTO provisions in general and removal of QRs in particular. SSIs did not get much time to adjust and
prepare themselves for increased competition and are thus in a precarious situation.
12.2   The Ministry has informed that it was pointed out by the industry that the imports from Nepal are basically re-
exports without any significant value addition to take advantage of the facility of 0% customs duty. The Committee is
also concerned that goods like Vanaspati are being imported which is adversely affecting the domestic producers. In the
absence of proper rules of origin, Nepal has become a re-export point for many of the products from China and other
South Asian countries. The provision of certificate of origin was dispensed with in the Indo-Nepal Treaty, which gave
rise to a spurt in flow of Chinese goods in the guise of Nepali goods. The Committee recommends that adequate
safeguards be taken to stop misuse of Indo-Nepal Treaty for import of goods from China and other countries.
12.3   Keeping in view the above situation, the provisions relating to value addition and certificate of origin have since
been incorporated in the renewed Treaty so as to protect the interests of Indian industry.
12.4   The Committee was also apprised that the Government has been closely monitoring the situation in this regard
and has taken steps to curb unfair trade practices leading to imports of under priced consumer goods from China. The
Directorate General of Anti-Dumping and Allied Duties has recommended Anti-Dumping final duty in 49 cases and
provisional duty has been recommended in 8 cases against Chinese goods. Further, 6 cases initiated against Chinese
goods are under investigation for preliminary findings.
12.5   A notification has been issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on 24.11.2000, requiring the
compliance of all the conditions of the Standards of Weights and Measures (Packaged Commodity) Order, 1977, on

117th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/117threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:27:03]
imports.
12.6   The Union Budget 2002-2003 has incorporated Section 8C in the Customs Tariff Act 1975 in terms of which
Central Government has been empowered to impose transitional product specific safeguard duty on import from the
People's Republic of China.
12.7   The Committee was informed that India's imports from China have not increased significantly and the imports
from China were Rs. 4613 crores during 1998-1999, which increased to Rs. 6706.3 crores during 2000-2001. However,
exports of India to China have grown from Rs. 1797.04 crores (1998-1999) to Rs. 3788.8 crores (2000-2001).
12.8   The Committee observes that the major option for limiting imports that remains for use by policy-makers in a
QR-free regime is that of higher tariffs. The Committee recommends that QRs may be converted into tariff and non-
tariff equivalents to give an adequate protection to the domestic SSIs. While this measure would be a discouraging
factor for foreign producers to export their cheap goods to India, it would also mean increasing revenue for the
Government of India.
12.9   The Committee recommends that on account of almost all products coming under Open General License (OGL)
list, the Government may further strengthen the anti-dumping mechanism so that remedial measures may be initiated
expeditiously. Countervailing duties and safeguard duties may be imposed in order to protect domestic producers from
cheap imports.
12.10 The Committee, therefore, recommends tariff and non-tariff barriers may be imposed in the form of higher safety
standards, and sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures as are permissible within the WTO framework.
12.11 The Committee further recommends that compulsory printing of manufacturing date, maximum retain price (in
Indian rupees) and composition of the products, by foreign exporters should be introduced. This would, of course, be
compatible with the national obligation under WTO, as domestic manufacturers are already required to comply with
these requirements.
XIII.   SICKNESS IN SSI SECTOR
13.1   To tackle the problem of rehabilitation of potentially viable sick SSI units, the RBI constituted a Working Group
on 25th November, 2000, under the chairmanship of Shri S.S. Kohli, the then Chairman of Indian Banks Association, to
look into the issue. The Working Group submitted its Report in May 2001. All the major recommendations of the
Working Group have been accepted by the RBI, including a change in the definition of sick SSI units, norms for
deciding on the viability of sick units, etc. The revised definition would enable Banks to take action at an early stage for
revival of the units. Based on the accepted recommendations of the Working Group, the RBI has drawn up the Revised
Guidelines for Rehabilitation of Sick SSI Units, which have been circulated on 16th January 2000, to all the Banks for
implementation.
13.2   The Ministry has informed that as per the latest data available from the RBI, out of 1,77,336 sick SSI units as at
the end of March 2002, 4493 units were identified as potentially viable. Out of these, 621 units were under nursing
programme. The concerned banks in accordance with the extent RBI determine the rehabilitation package for the
potentially viable sick SSI units, which is an ongoing process and the banks' efforts in this direction are continuing. As
per the data made available by the RBI, out of 13,076 potentially viable sick SSI units as on 31st March, 2001,
rehabilitation package has been approved in respect of 1254 units. Further, out of 753 units put under nursing as on 31st
March, 2001, 374 units have shown improvement as reported by banks.
13.3   Based on the recommendations of the Working Group constituted under the chairmanship of Shri S.S. Kohli, the
then Chairman of Indian Banks' Association, the RBI has drawn up revised guidelines for rehabilitation of sick SSI
units, which include inter-alia change in the definition of sick SSI units, norms for deciding on their viability, etc. The
RBI has circulated the revised guidelines on 16th January, 2002, to all the Scheduled Commercial banks for
implementation.
13.4   In order to revive sick industries, the Committee recommends that:
          I.      A special fund may be created for rehabilitation of sick SSIs and the commercial banks may earmark a
portion of loans to ailing SSIs.
          II.     The State Level Inter Institutional Committees (SLIICs) need to be revitalized and DICs may be used as a
forum to redress the grievances regarding delays in rehabilitation.
          III.   Local committees should be formed between the State Government and SSI Association and Banks to sort
out the credit related issues at local level.
          IV.   The Committee reiterates its observations given in its 75th Report that an Arbitration Clause may also be

XIV.  PROJECT SCHEMES FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE NE AREAS AND SIKKIM
14.1   The Ministry apprised the Committee that during the year 2002-03, the Plan Budget allocation (BE) for the
Ministry of Small Scale Industries was Rs. 350 crores. As per instructions, 10% of the total grant, i.e., Rs. 35 crores has
been put in the non-lapsable account for the North Eastern Region and Sikkim to meet the expenditure on various Plan

Guarantee Fund Scheme, Integrated Infrastructural Development Scheme, National Small Industries Corporation
(NSIC), Small Industries Service Institute (SISI), Entrepreneurship Development Programme (EDP), Management

implemented for overall development of Small Scale and Tiny Industries in the North Eastern States and Sikkim. These
Schemes are on-going schemes and promotional in nature. The BE provision of Rs. 35 crores has, however, been
reduced to Rs. 28.50 crore at the RE stage.
14.2   In the course of deliberation, the attention of the Committee was drawn to the Clause 146 of the Finance Bill,
2003 adversely affecting the benefit of exemption given to manufacturing units in North Eastern Region in relation to
Central Excise Exemption. The exemption of Central Excise Duty was granted for manufacturing units in Assam and
Tripura in July 1999, which was subsequently withdrawn on December 31, 1999 and restored on January 17, 2000. It
was subsequently extended to Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, and Manipur on March 1, 2000 and November 9, 2000.
The benefit from Pan Masala containing Tobacco and chewing Tobacco was withdrawn on March 1, 2001. The
Committee feels that the withdrawal of the benefits of Central Excise Exemption given to the North Eastern Region will
not only shake the confidence of the investors of the Pan Masala containing Tobacco, chewing Tobacco and Oil
Industry, but also of other sectors as the Government can also possibly withdraw excise exemption on their products
retrospectively and claim recovery. In fact the recent proposed amendment has cast a serious doubts into the minds of
investors and people of North Eastern Region towards the credibility of the Government of India.
14.3   The Committee is of the opinion that due to locational disadvantage and peculiar set up of the North Eastern
Region, industries which have set up for full fledged establishments in the North Eastern Region should be given the
benefit of Excise Duty exemption to generate employment in the region. The Committee notes that Finance Minister
informed the Rajya Sabha on 6th May, 2003 that some legal questions had arisen regarding chewing tobacco. The
Finance Minister assured the House that he would take action after obtaining legal advice in the matter. The Committee
observes that while giving exemption to excise duty in the North East, the Government should see as to whether such
units have employment potential and consistent with our tobacco policy.
XV.    EXCISE DUTY EXEMPTION
15.1   Excise exemption makes SSI products cost effective and strengthens their competitiveness. Excise exemption was
enhanced from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 1 crore in September 2001.
15.2   The representatives of Erode Handloom Cloth Merchant's Association informed the Committee that in the recent
budget CENVAT is introduced in the weaving sector and the exemption granted and the specified processes are
withdrawn if done with the add of power or steam. The powerloom weaving is a highly decentralized tiny sector. It
gives employment opportunity to lakhs of people in the country. The new introduction of CENVAT system will reduce
the excise duty of the mill sector, but levies duty on small traders. The result will be an encouragement to the
millionaires and blow to the poor traders. Under these circumstances, lakhs of people will be thrown out of employment.
15.3   The Representative of Tiruchengodu Taluk Small Powerloom Owner's Association stated that the Powerloom
sector fulfils the textile demand of the country and earns foreign exchange and shares 40% of the export of the country.
It is important to be pointed out that this powerloom sector has been functioning without any subsidy or monetary
assistance either from the Union Government or State Government. Powerloom owners are already paying excise duty
on the purchase of yarn to the tune of 9.2%. Owing to the excise duty and other duties paid at different stages until the
yarn become garments ready for use, the production cost has increased but the marketing is not proportionately
satisfactory. The announcement of 10% CENVAT on the production of powerloom to be implemented from April 1,
2000, will cripple the industry.

15.4   The Representatives of Somanpur Powerloom Cloth Manufactures Association stated that implementation of
VAT on powerloom sector should be deferred till 2005 and excise duty on cotton fabrics should be exempted. The
Government should provide support for modernisation of this sector. The readymade garments are mainly manufactured
by the units belonging to unorganized sector functioning at rented or own small space. Maximum of the entrepreneurs
finding no other employment opportunities, have started manufacturing garments and manage all activities including
procurement of raw materials, production, marketing, distribution and overall administration by themselves. It is not
understood why the readymade garment industry has been singled out for withdrawing SSI exemption so long enjoying
by them. The small units are not able to avail of the benefit under CENVAT Scheme, as the units are unorganized. The
units do not avail their inputs direct from the organized mills. Maximum of the units procure fabrics and other
accessories from the dealers at the 3rd or 4th stages and generally on the basis of daily requirements, which are at time
even 100 to 500 meters of fabrics whereas large units procure fabrics direct from the organized mills and avail the
benefit of CENVAT. The low profile readymade garment units in the State can hardly bear the excise burden as
imposed under the Union Budget for 2003-04, if the SSI exemption for readymade garments is not withdrawn, the
industry can hardly withstand the competition being faced by them on account of legal and illegal entry of readymade
garments from Nepal and Bangladesh. The Industry apprehends that West Bengal will ultimately be the market for
readymade garments of Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and China. Entrepreneurs engaged in Garment Industry will close
their units and turn to import garments legally or legally from those countries and market the same in India, which will
ultimately wipe out the labour intensive garment in the country. The garment industry will be wiped out if the SSI
excise exemption, as proposed, is withdrawn ultimately rendering about 10 crores of people employed directly or
indirectly in garment industry out of employment.
15.5   The Finance Minister in his Budget speech on Finance Bill, 2003 stated, "The Government wanted to totally
protect the interests of the small and the self-employed weavers and garment manufacturers. The Government had
significantly reduced customs duty on textiles machinery and reduced it upto 5 per cent on specified machinery. The
Government had announced a modernization package for powerlooms. The Government had also announced a financial
and technical package for the modernization of the entire textile industry like the Government had done it for the steel
industry. It has done in order to complete the CENVAT chain, to eliminate deemed credit and, finally to improve the
country's international ranking in the textiles industry. The Government had a total textile production of Rs. 3,775 crore.
Out of that Rs. 3,600 crore, by these figures were being exported.
          It is possible that a number of powerloom owners who are self-employed have up till now not filed any income
tax return. But they may now wish, therefore, either to declare their stocks for CENVAT purpose or to join the chain.
Therefore, to encourage them and new assesses of the powerloom sector or the garments to come into the mainstream,
the Income Tax Department has been instructed to encourage the powerloom owners to declare their stocks. If it does
not exceed Rs. 10,000 per powerloom, such declaration will not be subject to any questioning, any scrutiny or any other
inquiry. The Government purpose to fully exempt excise duty on unprocessed fabrics upto the first clearance of Rs.
20.00 lakh provided they are woven by powerloom units having an annual turnover of Rs. 25 lakh. It means that the
powerloom owners or the operators operating some of the traditional powerloom, not the modern variety, and holding
up to almost 10 powerlooms, will be totally free from excise duty. It is totally exempted upto Rs. 20 lakh. The tax of Rs.
5.00 lakh will be charged on Rs. 20-25 lakhs. The Government has given very strict instructions that there would be no
visit and no inspection to these powerlooms. The Government has introduced a self-assessment scheme so that these
powerloom owners could give their own self-assessment.
          The Government also propose to fully exempt from excise duty unbranded woven and knitted readymade
garments upto the first level of Rs. 25 lakh provided that annual turnover does not exceed Rs. 30 lakh. Such units would,
however, be required to keep only one record and it is a record of the yarn or fabric that they have purchased. The
Government has a tax research unit.
          The tax research unit has the details of all garment producers in the country. The Government find that almost
about 85 per cent of the garment manufacturers are in this Rs. 20.00 lakh to Rs. 25.00 lakh bracket. Those that are above
this are really major garment producers. They are not self-employed. The Government also proposes to extend this
exemption scheme to garments of rubberized textile fabrics, cotton benching, mosquito nets and fabrics of mono-
filament."
15.6   The Committee hopes that the above incentives announced by the Government would to a great extend benefit the
small-scale industry units engaged in powerloom and readymade garment sector. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry of Small Scale Industry should make a study of the impact of the above incentives on the Small Scale Industry
units and inform the Department-related Standing Committee on Industry about the same.
XVI.  MARKETING AND EXPORTS
16.1   Marketing, for both domestic and export markets, has all along been a major problem area for the small-scale

industry. Though the Price and Purchase Preference Policy has been in existence for a long time, there is need to take
several other measures.
16.2   Finance is a major area, which small-scale units report as a major impediment for marketing. The credit extended
by the units to their customers, to the trade and to the Government departments, and public sector enterprises, blocks a
major part of their funds.
16.3   Market Development Assistance (MDA) Programme has been launched for SSI Associations for participating in
international fairs, exhibitions, collection of information on marketing/exports, conducting surveys for filing anti-
dumping cases etc.
16.4   Marketing is an integral part of any commercial ventures. The Committee recommends that banks and other
financial institutions provide marketing oriented financial assistance to small-scale sector, particularly for advertising,
product promotion and setting up of regional marketing offices. Factoring services by the banks may also be given
greater priority. The Committee further recommends that Sector specific export thrust/policy measures and more Export
Promotion Zones should be established.
XVII. TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION
17.1   The technological upgradation of the SSI units in India has been quite slow. There are a number of factors that are
responsible for this. The Indian market has so far been basically a sellers' market. Therefore, entrepreneurs have not
made any efforts for modernisation. Moreover, there is non-availability of proper information regarding latest
technologies and their suppliers. There is inadequate availability of credit for investment in technological upgradation
and testing facilities are also not readily available. Even the technological institutions set up for assisting the small-scale
industries themselves lacks sophistication and coordination amongst each other.
17.2   The Ministry apprised the Committee that the number of units benefited under Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme for
Technology Upgradation upto 31st March 2002, was 6, and the amount of Subsidy disbursed was Rs. 25.95 lakhs.
However, during 2002-03 (upto February, 2003), 37 more units have availed subsidy totalling to Rs. 84.88 lakhs.
Though the progress of this Scheme has been slow initially, it has picked up momentum subsequently. However, there is
a need to further accelerate the pace of subsidy off-take under the Scheme. The following measures have been taken in
this regard :
          (i)     The progress of implementation of the Scheme is constantly monitored by a Governing and Technology
Approval Board (GTAB).
          (ii)    A Technical Sub-Committee has been constituted under the Chairmanship of Addl. Secretary and
Development Commissioner (SSI) for suggesting the inclusion of new sub-sectors/products and well
established and improved technologies under the Scheme.
          (iii)   Revised guidelines have been prepared by the Technical Sub-Committee. The salient features thereof are as
underlined:
                  a.     Number of eligible products/sub-sectors increased from 14 to 21.
                  b.     Number of eligible Primary Lending Institutions (PLIs) increased by addition of 34 Cooperative Banks
and 21 Regional Rural Banks for which NABARD will be the new Nodal Agency.
                  c.     In-house testing and on-line qualitative control equipments now eligible for assistance.
                  d.     Units availing subsidy under Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation of the
Small Scale Industries (CLCSS) shall not avail any other subsidy for Technology upgradation from the
Central/State/UT Governments.
                  e.     Release of subsidy will be to the extent of 50% with the first instalment of the loan and the balance 50%
with the last instalment.
                  f.      The term "Proven Technology" replaced by "Well-established and Improved Technology".
                  g.     List of Proven (now termed as "Well-established and Improved") Technologies expanded by adding six
new technologies.
          (iv)   Seminars and awareness programmes are organized to popularize the scheme.
17.3   For effective technological upgradation in Indian SSI units, the Committee recommends that the partnership
approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises be strengthened.
17.4   Technology Bureau for International Industrial Partnerships and Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises, Delhi
has been providing useful services for technology upgradation in the small-scale units. These organisations need to be

117th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/117threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:27:03]
strengthened further and their activities need to be marketed/advertised in an effective manner. The small-scale
industries in India have added strength to the industrial infrastructure and have been the engine of growth for
industrialisation. However, they are known for producing poor quality products. This makes the Indian goods less
competitive in the international markets.
17.5   The Committee observes that Government has set up a number of organizations for the purpose of technological
upgradation and quality improvement in the SSI units. However, the impacts of these facilities are not adequately felt.
The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective and beneficial to the
small industries.
17.6   The Committee further recommends that training to significantly improve quality by creating awareness among
personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and enforcing technical
discipline should be institutionalized. There is a need to conduct a comprehensive research study of SSI units to
determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop methodology for quality improvement and cost
reduction programmes. Further ISO 9000 certification, may be made more attractive to introduce quality-consciousness
among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be upgraded from time to time in tune with the developments in
quality worldwide.
XVIII.        LABOUR REFORMS IN SSIs
18.1   The Committee has been getting requests from various Industry Associations on the need to implement labour
reforms so as to make the SSI sector competitive. The Association representing the SSI sector have also time and again
stressed upon the need to free the SSI sector of archaic labour laws and also to free the SSI sector from the Inspector
Raj.
18.2   In this context the Committee observes that the present structure of labour laws does not encourage efficient
performance by the SSIs Managements find it difficult to manage their human resources optimally because of the
constrained labour laws. As of now, the same set of labour laws is applicable to all industrial undertakings, irrespective
of their size.
18.3   The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with simple
provision understandable by the entrepreneurs of SSI units be legislated. SSI units employing upto 50 persons should be
kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to govern the
relationship between the Employer and the Employee has to be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments Act
may also be suitably modified so as to adapt itself to the needs of the present day SSI sector.
18.4   The Committee further observes that the existing social security legislations such as Employees' Provident Fund
& Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Employees State Insurance Act, Maternity Benefits Act, Workmen's Compensation
Act, and the Payment of Gratuity Act are very cumbersome for entrepreneurs of small-scale units to understand and
comply with. The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of so many social security legislations, a
comprehensive Social Security Scheme be formulated on a priority basis for providing for one insurance cover to each
workman. The Committee strongly feels that the small-scale units should be able to devote more time to quality
management rather than inspector management.
XIX.  MULTIPLICITY OF AGENCIES
19.1   The Committee observes that at present, there are several Government agencies to deal with small-scale industries
in India. These include Ministry of SSI & ARI, Office of Development Commissioner (SSI), Small Industries
Development Organisation, Small Industries Service Institutes, National Small Industries Corporation, Small Industries
Development Bank of India, Product-cum-process Development Centres, Regional Testing Centres, District Industries
Centres, State Financial Corporations, State Industrial Development Corporations, State Small Industries Development
Corporations, etc.
19.2   The Committee, therefore, recommends that roles of all these organisations be re-evaluated and clearly defined. It
needs to be ensured that their activities do not overlap each other. There should also be co-ordination in the activities of
these agencies. Most importantly, all of these should be able to provide effective service to the small-scale sector.
XX.    DE-RESERVATION OF SSI ITEMS
20.1   The Union Minister for Commerce announced the removal of restrictions while announcing the EXIM policy for
2002-07. While the impact of the removal of QRs is being felt directly by industries, which were earlier protected, there
is likely to be greater impact on the SSIs, especially with regard to their competitive ability and integration with the
global markets against the opportunities of an expanding global market.
20.2   The policy of reservation, was not brought as a measure of protection alone, but was brought for some other

117th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/117threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:27:03]
factors as well as provisions of employment opportunities, development of industrial activities in the backward and rural
areas, utilization of local raw-materials, restraining migration of labour etc. Large industries and MNCs are not barred
from manufacturing the reserved items. They have only to adhere to the stipulation that 50% of their production of the
reserved items should be exported, which they could easily do with their latest technologies and their professional
management.
20.3   De-reservation of over 50 items which were marked for exclusive production in the SSI sector has hit hard such
affected and related units. The Committee fails to see any supportive and promotional measure in the latest Budget for
such affected units. It is to be noted that the Government had accepted the Abid Hussain Committee Report in full in
1997. The Abid Hussain Committee recommended that the abolition of reservation should accompany a support
package for the small industries, which include equity support, interest rate concessions, technology assistance etc. The
Abid Hussain Committee, therefore, recommended allocation of Rs. 500 crore per year i.e. Rs. 2,500 crore over the next
five years for the purpose.
20.4   The Ministry apprised the Committee that SSI reservation is in respect of manufacturing only. Export
opportunities on the other hand are a function of marketing for which there is no reservation. Even a reserved item can
be manufactured by a non-SSI unit when it undertakes to export more than 50% of its production. In any case, out of the
total of about 8,000 items being manufactured in the SSI sector, only 749 items are currently reserved and a further de-
reservation of 75 items has been announced in the Union Budget 2003-04.
20.5   Phased de-reservation of 881 items relating to laboratory chemicals and re-agents, leather and leather products,
plastic products, chemicals and chemical products and paper products is in tandem with the recommendations made by
various expert committees. It is desirable that the ceiling of investment in plant and machinery for manufacture of such
products is also increased to a limit of Rs. 5 crore to enable those units for taking up capacity expansion,
technology/upgradation/modernization and export promotion.
20.6   As such, no adverse impact on export can be attributed to the policy of reservation. Government constantly
reviews the situation through a conscious policy of fostering dialogue with stakeholders and putting in place support
measures as required.
20.7   The Committee feels that the Government should have given a support package to the affected units before doing
away with the reservation for such SSI units. The Committee recommends that this may include timely and low cost
credit; export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time frame may be
simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival. In the absence of such package, the
Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive. Moreover, effecting de-reservation without any package
will bring deleterious socio-economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic growth.
XXI.  INTEGRATED INFRASTRUCTURAL DEVELOPMENT SCHEME  (IIDS)
21.1   Small Industries Development Organisation (SIDO), Ministry of Small Scale Industries, Government of India has
been operating a number of promotional schemes for the growth of the small-scale industries in the country. The
Integrated Infrastructural Development Scheme is one such Scheme to facilitate the location of industries in rural
backward areas and to generate employment opportunities by establishing close linkages between agriculture and
industry.
21.2   IID Scheme is a Central Sector Scheme in which the Central Government and SIDO contribute to each IID Centre
Rs. 5.00 crore in the ratio of 2: 3 and the cost in excess thereof is met by State/UT Governments. Suitable land for this
purpose has to be provided by the State Government and this cost is not included in estimated cost of Rs. 5 crores.
21.3   The Committee recommends that unless State Governments play a proactive role in creating infrastructure for
industries, integration and harmonization of villages with industrial development cannot be achieved. Active
participation of State Governments, NGOs and SSI Associations should be ensured by providing appropriate
encouragement to them. This is in keeping with the Industrial Policy announced in 1991, to give special thrust to the
promotion and strengthening of small, tiny and village industries.
XXII. DELAYED PAYMENT TO SSIs
22.1   The Committee observes that the Delayed Payment to SSIs by large company continues to be a major problem for
SSIs sector. SSI Association informed the Committee that there is a 'Delayed Payment Act' to sort out the problems but
that has failed to give the desired results. SSI associations have also been suggesting that some punitive action be taken
against those large companies, which make undue delay in making payment to the small scale sector. Whenever they
file their income tax returns, certain amount should be charged from them. If there is some outstanding bill and they
have not paid them on account of delay payment, that amount should be adjusted at the time of filing the returns.
22.2   The Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, during oral evidence of

117th Report of Committee on Industry

Secretary, Ministry of Small Scale Industries, stressed upon problems of delayed payment and stated that many
complaints have been made by SSI Association in this regard.
22.3   The Representatives of Federation of Indian Small and Medium Enterprises (FISME), during their oral evidence
before the Committee, stated that Parliament passed a Bill called Delayed Payments Bill, but unfortunately the
jurisdiction of that Bill does not cover the Government organizations. It pertains to private sector only. The Government
Departments are not adhering to the payment schedule and the problem of delayed payment remain as it is.
22.4   The Committee, therefore, recommends that Comptroller and Auditor General should be advised to devise some
system so that the payments due to SSI are automatically paid within a specified time.
22.5   The Committee is of the opinion that the timely payment to SSIs could be ensured by issuing an appropriate
circular of the Ministry of Finance for the Ministries/Departments at least of the Central Government. The Central
Government should also impress upon the State Governments to take similar measures to expedite payments to SSIs.
22.6   The Committee reiterates its recommendation that stringent action should be taken against the erring large
companies which have failed to make payment to SSIs in due time. Necessary amendment for taking punitive action
may also be contemplated in the Delayed Payment Act.
XXIII.        PURCHASE PREFERENCE FOR SSI SECTOR
24.1   In USA, there are special laws for small-scale sector. But in our country, there is no such provision for small-scale
sector. Moreover, 50 items have been de-reserved which were exclusively reserved for the small-scale sector. Marketing
facilities for the small-scale sector are also not adequate. Majority of the consumption of items manufactured by small-
scale sector is for domestic consumption. Only 8-10% of the items made by SSIs are exported.
24.2   The Committee reiterates its recommendation, made in its 75th Report, that in order to protect small scale sector
from multinational companies and others, a certain per cent of items, say 33% should be purchased from SSI sector by
Central and State Government Departments/Agencies specially when the items reserved for SSI sector have been
withdrawn and majority of the items have been put on OGL list. The policy of purchase preference system as followed
by USA Government for protection of indigenous industries may be emulated. Necessary action in this regard should be
initiated by the Ministry of SSI immediately.
XXIV.        LIMITED PARTNERSHIP ACT
25.1   Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) in its written memorandum stated that Issues that presently
the partners in a partnership 551 unit have unlimited liabilities resulting from the activities and liabilities of the 551
units. Hence Limited Partnership Act should be inacted which, in turn, will limit the liability of the partners to their
equity contribution as well as facilitate bringing in external equity participation.
25.2   A mention has been made about the Partnership Act in the Union Budget 2003-04 and the Ministry of SSI is
addressing the matter. The Committee desired that the legislation should be enacted without much delay.
XXV. IMPACT OF GLOBALISATION AND LIBERALISATION ON SMALL SCALE SECTOR
26.1   The SSI sector continues to be a major generator of employment, next only to the agriculture sector. The sector
has been consistently meeting the targets fixed for employment generation. Given the vast employment opportunities in
the SSI sector, the Government has envisaged creation of 4.4 million additional jobs in this sector during the Tenth Five
Year Plan period (2002-07).
26.2   The Government is constantly monitoring the impact of globalisation and WTO arrangements on the economy
including SSIs and has put in several measures to safeguard the interests of domestic industry. These include special
focus on areas such as technology upgradation, infrastructure assistance through cluster approach, enhanced fiscal
support, timely availability of credit, adoption of modern management facilities, use of electronic infrastructure and
other IT applications to face the emerging challenges of trade liberalization. Protection of these industries is available in
the form of raising customs duties upto the bound levels, imposing anti-dumping duties and countervailing duties,
taking safeguard measures in case of surge in import etc.
26.3   While the globalization and liberalization have exposed the SSI sector to greater competition both domestically
and globally on the one hand, they have on the other provided the SSI sector greater access to markets, cheaper
imported raw materials and technologies. Keeping in view the available trends in employment, exports, production,
number of units etc., which indicate high rates of growth, no major visible adverse impact has been noticed on the SSI
sector.
26.4   With a view to provide a level playing field and help the SSI sector to compete in the international market, the
following measures have been taken by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries:

XXVI.  SINGLE "COMPREHENSIVE LAW"
27.1     Because of the complexities involved in the altering legal statues and the country's Constitutional separation of
Centre-State powers, the Central Government has appointed the Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI) to
propose, inter-alia, a draft of a Comprehensive law for Small Industries. The draft of the Small Enterprises
Development Bill, 2002 was tabled as an Agenda.
27.2     Deputy Director General, CII, during his oral evidence before the Committee stated that there should be "Single
Comprehensive Law" because small scale industry today is really bogged down with all kinds of pressures, the
Inspector-raj, various laws, various records that they are required to maintain. A comprehensive draft law has been
tabled at the last SSI Board meeting, which was then forwarded to various states, because most of these controls are
under the power of various States in India.
27.3     The Committee recommends that the Comprehensive law should be enacted. It should be an encompassing one
and should enable the SSI Sector to come out of the clutches of inspector raj. The Committee is of the opinion that
inspector raj has persisted despite attempt at the higher level to change it and time has come to enact suitable legislative
action to bring the inspector raj to an end.
XXVII.        SURVIVAL OF MINI CEMENT PLANTS
28.1     The Committee in its 81st Report discussed the problems relating to Mini Cement Plants. On receipt of a
representation of U.P. Mini Cement Owner's Association, Kanpur, the matter was again taken up with the Ministry of

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
          The Committee observes that in the era of globalisation and liberalisation of the economy, the Small Scale
Industries should be strengthened to compete in the international markets. Policy measures should be formulated and
relevant data should be obtained through surveys, investigations and studies. The Committee recommends that the role
of Development Commissioner for SSI should be oriented in accordance with the ever-changing scenario so as to make
the SSI sector internationally competitive.                                                                                                 (Para 3.5)
          The Committee further observes that it has become extremely essential to create awareness about India's
obligations under the WTO regime and their impact on various sectors. Having heard the representatives of Powerloom,
Readymade garment, Pan Masala Associations, the Committee draws an inference that there is some communication
gap between the SIDO and SSI Associations. Therefore the Committee recommends that there should be regular
interaction between the Government and Small Scale Industries. A Committee at local level should also be formed
between Bankers and local chapters of SSI Associations to sort out their problems relating to credit related issues at
local level in all the States. The local committee should give quarterly report to the Ministry of Small Scale Industries,
Ministry of Finance (Banking Division) and Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry.                            (Para 3.6)
          The Committee expresses its concerns on the role of NSIC in the small scale industry sector. The Committee feels
that the Corporation is still very much relevant in the present scenario and recommends that the Ministry should
wholeheartedly support its restructuring business plans and ensure that Corporation does not lose its focus i.e. providing
marketing and technology upgradation support to the small sector.                                      (Para 4.6)

power, fuel, raw materials and credit at reasonable prices should be provided to make SSIs more competitive. The
Committee further recommends that Cluster-wise tool rooms and CAD-CAM rooms should be set up. (Para 5.4)
          The Committee feels that the process of liberalization has exposed the Small Scale Industries (SSI) sector to
intensified competition both globally and domestically. In order to help building up the capabilities of the units in the
SSI sector to face the emerging challenges, there has to be a further increase in the flow of financial assistance to
facilitate additional capacity generation, expansion of the existing units and improving their capacity utilization,
diversification and to enhance the competitiveness of the sector with a thrust on technology upgradation and
modernization.    (Para 6.8)
          The Committee is of the opinion that there should be effective implementation of these schemes. Further, once a
loan has been sanctioned, a time frame for the release of various installments should be committed in accordance with
the needs of the entrepreneurs. The Committee also feels that it must also be ensured that with the provision of the
concept of single window, the time involved in making the disbursements is considerably reduced. As far as the
National Equity Fund (NEF) scheme is concerned, it may be noted that the disbursements under the scheme are very
small. The scheme needs to be made more effective and efficient.                                                                                   
(Para 6.13)
          The Committee recommends that cost of credit should be directly linked with the benchmarks achieved by a small
unit in terms of Financial, Marketing, Technical, Quality, and Environmental standards.            (Para 6.14)
          The Committee further observes that the implementation and enhancement in the limit for guaranteeing loans
under the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme should include the following :
          (a)    Time bound and effective implementation;
          (b)    Increase of corpus to Rs. 1250 crores over the next one year;
(c)    Enhancement in the maximum availing credit limit to Rs. 50 lakhs.  (Para 6.15)
          The Committee desired that the working of credit guarantee scheme and the availability of credit should be looked
upon as a major issue. The Committee observes that the amount of Rs. 397.56 crore for Credit Guarantee Scheme is
worth Rs. 172.80 crores is very thin inspite of the fact that this is main item on the budget of the Small Scale Industry
Ministry. The Committee strongly recommends for enhancement of allocation and impresses upon the Ministry of Small
Scale Industries to take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance and Planning
Commission.                                                                    (Para 7.8)
          The Committee further observes that credit facility is one of the basic inputs that have to be provided to SSIs if
they have to enhance their competitiveness in the era of globalisation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
banks should come forward in extending a helping hand to the small and tiny sector in sanctioning collateral free loan to
SSIs. The Committee also reiterates that income tax exemption may be provided to the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust of
the Small Industries to make it self-sustainable.                                                                                 (Para 7.9)
          The Committee recommends that more Venture funds should be set up for information technology, biotechnology
and food processing. The Committee feels that Venture Capital could be a successful concept in bringing out the latent
entrepreneurship spirit of the youth of the country. In this context the Committee recommends that a suitable policy
framework may be designed expeditiously to promote setting up of such funds in the public as well as the private sector.
Banks should be encouraged to entertain Venture Capital funding to SSI units.                                                              
          (Para 8.3)
          The Committee observes that removal of quantitative restrictions has brought Indian industry face-to-face with
foreign products, which are technologically for superior. Moreover, technical barriers to trade are emerging as major
non-tariff barriers to access the markets of the developed countries. Therefore, Indian Industry, particularly the SSI
sector, needs support to upgrade to the high technical standards set by the developed countries.              (Para 9.8)
          The Committee recommends that in order to initiate the activities of the proposed fund and run the same on
sustainable basis, initially a fund support of Rs. 20 crore may be provided by the Government of India to SIDBI. The

small scale sector and provide financial and support services to the SSIs with the help of existing credit delivery system
and support service agencies.                                                                                                 (Para 10.4)
          The Committee however, feels that the Central Government should establish a nodal agency, keeping in view the
interest of SSIs in particular and industry in general, in Ministry of Finance (preferably headed by an officer not below
the rank of Addl. Secretary) to coordinate implementation of VAT in States. There is a need to list the operative
problems in interstate transactions, which could only be solved with the intervention of the Central Government.       
(Para 11.3)
          The Committee further observes that the Central Government should act swiftly and decisively to bring in the
homogeneity in the States' VAT Acts : homogeneity in basic principles and classification.  (Para 11.4)
          The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance should develop an extensive information base in
Ministry's web site on VAT (or a separate site altogether to solve confusion arising out of lack of updated information at
one point.                  (Para 11.5)
          The Ministry has informed that it was pointed out by the industry that the imports from Nepal are basically re-
exports without any significant value addition to take advantage of the facility of 0% customs duty. The Committee is
also concerned that goods like Vanaspati are being imported which is adversely affecting the domestic producers. In the
absence of proper rules of origin, Nepal has become a re-export point for many of the products from China and other
South Asian countries. The provision of certificate of origin was dispensed with in the Indo-Nepal Treaty, which gave
rise to a spurt in flow of Chinese goods in the guise of Nepali goods. The Committee recommends that adequate
safeguards be taken to stop misuse of Indo-Nepal Treaty for import of goods from China and other
countries.                                             (Para 12.2)
          The Committee observes that the major option for limiting imports that remains for use by policy-makers in a
QR-free regime is that of higher tariffs. The Committee recommends that QRs may be converted into tariff and non-
tariff equivalents to give an adequate protection to the domestic SSIs. While this measure would be a discouraging
factor for foreign producers to export their cheap goods to India, it would also mean increasing revenue for the
Government of India.          (Para 12.8)
          The Committee recommends that on account of almost all products coming under Open General License (OGL)
list, the Government may further strengthen the anti-dumping mechanism so that remedial measures may be initiated
expeditiously. Countervailing duties and safeguard duties may be imposed in order to protect domestic producers from
cheap imports.                                                                                                                (Para 12.9)
          The Committee, therefore, recommends tariff and non-tariff barriers may be imposed in the form of higher safety
standards, and sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures as are permissible within the WTO framework.                             
          (Para 12.10)
          The Committee further recommends that compulsory printing of manufacturing date, maximum retail price (in
Indian rupees) and composition of the products, by foreign exporters should be introduced. This would, of course, be
compatible with the national obligation under WTO, as domestic manufacturers are already required to comply with
these requirements.          (Para 12.11)
          In order to revive sick industries, the Committee recommends that :
          I.      A special fund may be created for rehabilitation of sick SSIs and the commercial banks may earmark a
portion of loans to ailing SSIs.
          II.     The State Level Institutional Committees (SLIICs) need to be revitalized and DICs may be used as a forum
to redress the grievances regarding delays in rehabilitation.
          III.   Local committees should be formed between the State Government and SSI Association and Banks to sort
out the credit related issues at local level.
          IV.   The Committee reiterates its observations given in its 75th Report that an Arbitration Clause may also be
included in all borrower-lender arrangements in terms of Indian Arbitration Act to avoid protracted litigation
and costs. Although Entrepreneurship Development through small enterprises is basically owner-managed, a
significant number of them do employ persons for performing managerial functions. The SSI units on the
growth path should encourage their key personnel to think and work more as entrepreneurs than as mere
employees.                                                                                                                     (Para 13.4)
          The Committee is of the opinion that due to locational disadvantage and peculiar set up of the North Eastern

          The Committee hopes that the above incentives announced by the Government would to a great extent benefit the
small scale industry units engaged in powerloom and readymade garment sector. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry of Small Scale Industry should make a study of the impact of the above incentives on the Small Scale Industry
units and inform the Department-related Standing Committee on Industry about the
same.                                                                (Para 15.6)
          Marketing is an integral part of any commercial ventures. The Committee recommends that banks and other
financial institutions provide marketing oriented financial assistance to small scale sector, particularly for advertising,
product promotion and setting up of regional marketing offices. Factoring services by the banks may also be given
greater priority. The Committee further recommends that Sector specific export thrust/policy measures and more Export
Promotion Zones should be established.                                                                                                      (Para 16.4)
          For effective technological upgradation in Indian SSI units, the Committee recommends that the partnership
approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises be strengthened.                          (Para 17.3)
          The Committee observes that Government has set up a number of organizations for the purpose of technological
upgradation and quality improvement in the SSI units. However, the impacts of these facilities are not adequately felt.
The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective and beneficial to the
small industries.   (Para 17.5)
          The Committee further recommends that training to significantly improve quality by creating awareness among
personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and enforcing technical
discipline should be institutionalized. There  is a need to conduct a comprehensive research study of SSI units to
determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop methodology for quality improvement and cost
reduction programmes. Further ISO 9000 certification, may be made more attractive to introduce quality-consciousness
among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be upgraded from time to time in tune with the developments in
quality worldwide.          (Para 17.6)
          The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with simple
provisions understandable by the entrepreneurs of SSI units be legislated. SSI units employing upto 50 persons should
be kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to govern
the relationship between the Employer and the Employee has to be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments Act
may also be suitably modified so as to adapt itself to the needs of the present day SSI sector.                                             
(Para 18.3)
          The Committee further observes that the existing social security legislations such as Employees' Provident Fund
& Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Employees State Insurance Act, Maternity Benefits Act, Workmen's Compensation
Act, and the Payment of Gratuity Act are very cumbersome for entrepreneurs of small scale units to understand and
comply with. The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of so many social security legislations, a
comprehensive Social Security Scheme be formulated on a priority basis for providing for one insurance cover to each
workman. The Committee strongly feels that the small scale units should be able to devote more time to quality
management rather than inspector management.          (Para 18.4)
          The Committee, therefore, recommends that roles of all these organisations be re-evaluated and clearly defined. It
needs to be ensured that their activities do not overlap each other. There should also be co-ordination in the activities of
these agencies. Most importantly, all of these should be able to provide effective service to the small scale sector.          
          (Para 19.2)
          The Committee feels that the Government should have given a support package to the affected units before doing
away with the reservation for such SSI units. The Committee recommends that this may include timely and low cost
credit; export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time frame may be
simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival. In the absence of such package, the
Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive. Moreover, effecting de-reservation without any package
will bring deleterious socio-economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic
growth.                                              (Para 20.7)
