2.6              The Committee was of the opinion that the importa nce of the cottage and tiny industrial sectors 
for Himachal Pradesh  needs to be emphasised. It holds the key to large scale employment and
generation of economic activities in  remote areas. It is, therefore, proposed to enhance the opportunities
of employment and income in such activities. The traditional skills and  cultural heritage associated with
production in this sector will need to be preserved.

few districts and a large area of the State rema ins unaffected by industr ialisation. The Committee
recommends that new areas be developed and the process of Industrialisation spread in a manner so as to
benefit the State as a whole.

technical education are not adequa te in Himachal Pradesh. The Co mmittee recommends that the local
industry and State Government shoul d join hands to restructure trai ning programmes so as to provide
employment to the youth.

3.17     The Central Transport S ubsidy Scheme was introduced in the year 1971.  Under this scheme
75% freight from nearest rail head incurred on import of raw material from out side the State and export
of finished goods outside the St ate is reimbursed by the Central Government through  the State
Government  The scheme is applicable to No rth-Eastern States comp rising Assam, Meghalaya, 
Manipur, Nagaland, Tripura, Arunach al Pradesh, Mizoram, Sikkim and other States of Andaman and
Nicobar islands, Himachal PradeshPradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Uttaranchal. 
3.18.    As already mentioned above under the scheme 75%  cost of freight incurred from the nearest rail

was available to all the units.  However, vide notification No.II (1)95-DBA/11 dated 29 th September, 
1995 Government of India has extended the scheme up to March 2000 but restricted the subsidy to only
those units which have not completed first five year of production on the date of notification.

CHAPTER–I 
INDUSTRIAL SCENARIO IN THE NORTH EASTERN REGION 
1.0   The entire North East region is very sensitive and has been witnessing troubled socio-political 
disturbances since long.  As a consequence, the economic development has suffered badly, resulting in
poor industrial growth. 
1.1   The main reason for insurgency in the North East was the alienation of the people, which began
immediately after independence. The Government has taken some initiatives and a sizable number o f
insurgents have laid down arms. But immediately after, they have started looking for employment. 
Internal security problems cannot be resolved if such issues cannot be addressed. 
1.2   Every Government that has come to power at the center has been concerned about the developmen t
in the North East but progress has been rather ta rdy, if not stagnant, despite announcement of special
economic packages. In 1995, North East Development Bank with an authorized capital of Rs. 500 crores
was created but how far it has helped expansion and modernization of industrial enterprises is no t
known.  The region still lacks good roads, water and electricity, the basic needs for development. Wha t
can help boost growth is collection of unspent balance of the amounts earmarked for different Union
Ministries and spending of the same in the region with the emphasis on the feasible projects an d
sustaining the existing industries, which are facing diffi culties.  It has two objectives-one is the survival 
of the industry and the second is the generation of employment. The main objective is, however, the
reduction elimination of insurgency.  The existing units should be helped so that they can meet the social
obligation develop the area, generate employment. Everything should not be seen from the revenue poin t
of view. Unless existing industries survive, no investme nt from outside North East is likely to come as is
evident from the fact that after 1997 no new projects have come to the region. The fiscal concessions
along with peace initiative will change the economic climate of North East and bring it in the mainstream
of country and it will not be viewed as a distant territory. 
1.3   The Government of India had granted certain incentives to some specified industries located in the
North East.  These incentives were mainly in the form of excise duty relief and capital investmen t
subsidy. These incentives are applicable only for those started production after 24 th December 1997. The 
transport subsidy scheme 1971 was also included in the above policy. This step is in fact to encourage the
industrial growth in the North East Region. The underlying idea behind extending these incentives was to
provide the much needed impetus to the North Eastern States so that the region could overcome its
backwardness and the difficulties faced by it on account of geographical isolation and provide them a
level playing field.  The ultimate goal was to f acilitate setting up of new industries and sustain those,
which exist already and thus paving the way for all round economic development of the region. Howeve r
due to the incorporation of the cut-off date of 24th December 1997, a large section of the industries in the
area prior to this date were left uncovered by those well intended notification. 
STUDY OF HINDUSTAN PAPER CORPORATION LIMITED BY THE COMMITTEE ON
HEAVY INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES 
1.4   The Committee of Ministry of the Heavy Indus tries and Public Enterprises ( of the Departmen t
Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry ) was constituted in May 2000 which examine d
the performance of Hindustan Paper Corporation Limited and its units viz-Cachar Paper Mills (CPM ) 
and Nagaon Paper Mills (NPM) located in the State of Assam as a case study in the above background. 
1.5   While examining the subject matter, the followi ng points surfaced in the meetings held with the
workers’ unions and the management of the Company on the 9th July, 2000 at Kolkata.

and Revival.  However, the persuasive efforts of Department of Heavy Industries were not bearing much
fruit. Besides it was observed by the Committee that these issues needed to be approached through a
coordinated effort and moreover the Committee also felt that there was a lack of appreciation of concerns
expressed by the Department of Heavy Industry in re spect of HPC’s operation by the other ministries.  
The Committee feels that at the strategic level th e problems facing industrial units in the NE,
notwithstanding whether it is private or public sector, are uniform and similar. 
1.7   The issues like transport subsidy, excise duty exemption etc.  encompassed all the public and private
units. Hence, the Committee thought to be benefited by the public sector as well as the private secto r
located in the NE.  It heard the view of the indust ries in the NE both in the public and the private secto r
on 8th August, 2001.  It emanated from the views expr essed by these that not only were the problems o f
the units grave but it was being further aggravated by a Supreme Court order of 13 th December, 1996 
related to debarring private plantation in the NE whic h violated the constitutional guarnteed rights of the
local tribals of the NE under Article 371 A-C and 371-H of the Constitution. It came to the observation of

addressed on priority.  Realizing the gravity of the situation that Committee thereafter called upon the
Secretaries of Ministries of Environment and Fo rest, Law, Industrial Policy and Promotion, Banking
Revenue, Heavy Industry, Railways and the mana gement of HPC on 21 st August, 2001 with a view to

“The Government Policy has been that they have  given a one time incentive and some limited time
incentive for development of remote areas.  One time incentive has been in the shape of capital
subsidy and the limited time incentive in the shape of transport subsidy or excise duty exemption o r
sales tax concession.  For areas like the North East, there is a continuing disadvantage and if there is
a one-time incentive or a limited time incentive it has not taken care of the continuing disadvantage. 
There is always a need for transporting the finished goods because they cannot be consumed locally. 
There are some raw materials, which are to be brought in.  If the industries are to survive in the
North East region, then these incentives must be on a continuous basis.  It has generally been seen

Committee the following position with regard to the railway network in the North East Region: 
         "(i)    Cachar Paper Mill (CPM) operati ng in the Barak Valley at Panchgram, is connected by the
meter gauge (Lumding – Badarpur Hill section) to the railway network. When the mill was se t
up the understanding was that the by 1990 the broad gauge connectivity would cover Bara k 
Valley also. The conversion from meter gauge to broad gauge has so far taken place only upto 
Lumding. The transshipment at Lumding which is a relatively smaller junction, as compared to 
Guwahati, where earlier transhipments used to take place has caused a lot of problems fo r 
movement of bulk material inputs like coal, Ba mboo, industrial grade salt, etc. and of the 
finished products i.e. paper reels/sheet. 
         (ii)     The Lumding-Badarpur Hill section was completed in 1903. The Railways are not investing
in track renewal or rolling stock with regard to meter gauge sections owing to the fact that 
broad gauge connectivity is envisaged for the entire network.
 
         (iii)    The meter gauge track between Lumding and Badarpur/Silchar rests upon 586 bridges – 73 
major and 151 minor – and goes through 37 tunne ls. The track is vulnerable to breaches an d
landslides, especially during the monsoon period. 
         (iv)    The Lumding – Badarpur/Silchar meter gauge serves as the life line for supply of essential
goods to the people of Mizoram, Manipur and Tripura apart from the inhabitants of Bara k 
Valley in Assam. Movements of materials to CPM receives a much lower priority in view o f 
the freight traffic density.

loading advantage to the Railways. However, the number of rakes being made available to

 CHAPTER – V 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
SUBSIDY 
5.0   Under the new industrial policy for the No rth Eastern Region finalized by the Government in
December 1997, the units located in the North East sector are eligible for transport subsidy only for the
first five years of commercial production till 31.3.2007 in addition, all the units in those zones would be
free from income tax, excise duty, for a period of 10 years from the commencement of production. 
5.1   The rationale for transport subsidy is to mitigat e the high cost of transportation of raw material an d
finished products due to location of  units in remote, hilly and inaccessible areas of the country, where
infrastructure is poor. 
5.2   The transportation cost of NPM and CPM for raw materials and finished products from and to the
main land is extremely high and hence needs to be mitigated through extension of subsidy. The grant o
f
transport subsidy should be reviewed in a different light. While units through improved performance may
become economically viable even after tax holiday, the transportation cost does not get mitigated unless
the requisite infrastructure is developed. 
5.3   The southern part of Assam, where the CPM is  situated, is highly monsoon prone area and the roads
are inundated with flood water every years and land slides occur causing disruption of road movement for
about 2-3 months every year. Thus CPM deserves some fiscal concessions from the Government to
become a viable unit. 
5.4   HPC, therefore, appealed to the Government of India to include the existing establishment which are
continuously being affected adversely due to their locational disadvantages, like the CPM, under the new
industrial policy and grant extension of excise duty payment for a period of ten years and to revive the
transport subsidy scheme w.e.f. April 1995 as a special case for CPM.

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Thirty-second Report on the "MoU performance in respect of PSUs
of Power Sector, Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises)".
2.      The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises was constituted on the 6th January,
2003. This Sub-Committee has been examining the performance of MoU system in the PSUs and this report deals with
the performance of PSUs of the Power Sector.
3.      The report is based on the deliberations of the meetings held with the representatives of various PSUs and the oral
evidence of representatives of various Ministries at New Delhi on 5th August, 2003 and Chennai on 21st September,
2003.
4.      The Committee at its meeting held on 18th December, 2003 considered and adopted the Report..
NEW DELHI
18 December, 2003
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry.
REPORT
CHAPTER-I
MoU SYSTEM
1.      The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a negotiated document between the Government, acting as the
owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific PSE. It contains the intentions, obligations and mutual
responsibilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MoU makes an attempt to move the management of PSEs from
management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.
1.2    The genesis of the policy of Memorandum of Understanding can be traced to the report of the Arjun Sengupta
Committee. One of the recommendations of this Committee was for the introduction of the system of MoU for
measurement of performance of public enterprises.
OBJECTIVES OF THE MoU SYSTEM
1.3    The objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy
and accountability of the management; to remove the fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise to pursue
through clearly laid down performance targets in the MoU and to enable the evaluation of managerial performance
through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to
stimulate improved performance.

132nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/132ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:43:05]
1.4    Under the agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the
year. Thus the MoU covers both financial performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this system
performance of the Company is categorized into five categories namely; excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor.
PREPARATION OF MoU
1.5    Based on the guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) in the month of October/November,
the draft MoUs are prepared by PSEs and forwarded to the Administrative Ministry and DPE by December. The draft
MoUs indicate the performance targets on a five point scale as proposed by the PSE for the ensuring financial year for
all crucial parameters like production, sales, profits, etc. The PSEs are also expected to include dynamic parameters of
significance for strengthening the future potential of the enterprise, such as project implementation, R&D, Human
Resource Development, etc. Appropriate weights are assigned to each of these parameters. The draft MoU are discussed
with the PSE Administrative Ministries at the Adhoc Task Force (ATF) negotiation meetings arranged in DPE in the
month of March/April, soon after the presentation of the Union Budget. Since the Budget has implications on the
performance targets, the timing of the negotiation meetings is deliberately scheduled after the budget presentation. The
appropriateness of the parameters and weights and the soundness of the targets as also the commitments of the
Government are examined in detail at the negotiation meetings. The draft MoUs as finalised thereafter are placed before
the High Power Committee (HPC) comprising the Cabinet Secretary as Chairman, Secretary, Finance. Planning
Commission, Programme Implementation, Chairman Public Enterprises Selection Board, Chief Economic Adviser and
Secretary Public Enterprises as Members, for approval. After approval, they are signed by the respective Chief
Executives and Secretaries.
EVALUATION OF MoU
1.6    The evaluation of the MoU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Ad-hoc Task Force (ATF) on
the basis of actual achievement vis-a-vis the MoU targets. Where the performance exceeds the targets by the pre-
determined stipulated level the enterprise is ranked as ‘excellent’ and when the target is just met, the enterprise is ranked
as ‘very good’. In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either ‘good’ or ‘fair’ or ‘poor’.
Ranking depends on how the performance has been as compared to MoU targets.
1.7    The performance criteria should be assigned appropriate weights corresponding with their stated priorities in the
objectives. It should be ensured that they also reflect the perceived relative importance of the various criteria in the
judgement of the PSE/Ministry. The weight for physical criteria should be kept as low as possible. Instead, Efficiency
and Dynamic criteria should get higher weights. The weight for profit-related financial parameters would be 60% in
case of PSEs operating under free market mechanism. The weight of 60% would be distributed to, Gross Margin, Gross
Profit/Capital Employed and Net Profit/Net Worth, each having a weight of 20% each. For PSEs operating under
administered prices, PSEs where Government is sole/almost sole customer and Trading, Consultancy, Engineering and
Financial PSEs, the weight would be 40%. The weight of 40% would be distributed to, Gross Margin and Net Profit/Net
Worth, each having a weight of 20% each. The PSEs which have been specially set up for implementing certain
Government policy directives will have no pre-determined financial parameters.
1.8    The targets set should be realistic and growth oriented. It should be insured that the MoU targets flow from the
Corporate Vision/Plans formulated by the PSEs and there is linkage between them. In case there is any variation,
reasons thereof should be clearly specified. For qualitative indicators, the targets for each of the points on the 5-point
scale should be indicated in the performance matrix itself. If these targets are on a time scale, only such target which fall
within the MoU year is included.
1.9    The MOU should contain the past five years performance data on criteria included in the MoU in an appendix. It
should also indicate the projections for the next five years, as far as possible consistent with the corporate plan.
POWER SECTOR
1.10  Power is a critical infrastructure for economic development and for improving the quality of life. The achievement
of increasing installed power capacity from 1362 MW to over 100,000 MW since independence and electrification of
more than 500,00 villages is impressive in absolute terms. However, it is a matter of concern that the annual per capita
consumption of India, at about 350 kwh is among the lowest in the world. Further, people in a large number of villages
have no access to electricity. The end users of electricity like households, farmers, commercial establishments,
industries are confronted with frequent power cuts, both scheduled and unscheduled. Power cuts, erratic voltage and low
or high supply frequency have added to the power woes of the consumer. These problems emanate from:---
         (i)     Inadequate power generation capacity;
         (ii)     Lack of optimum utilization of the existing generation capacity;

132nd Report of Committee on Industry

         (iii)    Inadequate inter-regional transmission links;
         (iv)    Inadequate and ageing sub-transmission and distribution network leading to power cuts and local
failures/faults;
         (v)    Large scale theft and skewed tariff structure;
         (vi)    Slow pace of rural electrification;
         (vii)   Inefficient use of electricity by the end consumer; and
         (viii)  Lack of grid discipline.
1.11  The Committee has been examining the performance of the PSEs in terms of the MoU of various sectors. The
Committee under took this study of MoU performance in respect of PSUs of Power sector and interacted with the
representatives of National Thermal Power Corporation Limited (NTPC) at New Delhi on the 5th August, 2003 and
Neyveli Lignite Corporation Limited (NLC) and Power Grid Corporation of India Limited at Chennai on the 21st
September, 2003.
CHAPTER-II
NATIONAL THERMAL POWER CORPORATION LIMITED (NTPC)
2.0    The National Thermal Power Corporation Limited (NTPC) was incorporated in November, 1975 with the
objective of planning, promoting and organizing integrated development of thermal power in the country and has a
Vision: “To be one of the World’s largest and best power utilities, powering India’s growth”. NTPC is schedule ‘A’
Navratan Company having a total approved investment of Rs.63,242.16 crores. NTPC has an approved capacity of
26,755 MW. The authorized capital of the Corporation is Rs.10,000 crores.
2.1    The Corporation has under operation/implementation coal based super thermal power plants/projects at thirteen
locations namely Singrauli (UP), Rihand (UP), NCTPP Dadri (UP), Korba (Chhattisgarh), Vindhyachal (MP),
Ramagundam (AP), Farakka (WB), Kahalgaon (Bihar), Talcher-Kaniha (Orissa), Talcher (Orissa), Unchahar (UP).
Simhadri (A.P.) and Tanda (UP) and combined cycle gas power projects at seven locations namely Anta (Rajasthan),
Auraiya (UP), Dadri (UP), Kawas (Gujarat), Jhanor-Gandhar (Gujarat), Kayamkulam (Kerala) and Faridabad
(Haryana). In addition NTPC is implementing its first hydro electric power project namely Koldam HEPP (800 MW).
The NTPC has already commissioned 20,935 MW. In addition to this, NTPC has taken over 314 MW of Captive power
Plants at Durgapur, Rourkela and Bhilai Steel Plants of SAIL through formation of 50:50 equity participation Joint
ventures between NTPC and SAIL. Thus, the total installed capacity of NTPC is 21249 MW. Apart from this, Badarpur
Thermal Power Station (705 MW), which is a major source of power supply to Delhi is being managed by NTPC on
behalf of Government of India.
MoU SYSTEM IN NTPC
2.2    NTPC was one of the very few companies that was picked up in the first lot for introduction of MoU system. And,
over a period of time, with reference to the MoU system that was introduced, improvements were made in this
instrument itself. And today, the NTPC is not only a Navratna but has become a Navratna Company sanctioning its own
projects. Since this instrument was introduced, the NTPC has always been categorised in the group of excellent
performers. They have emerged as one of the top most power-generating companies in the world.

the number of Government Directors on the Board from what it used to be in the past, and brought people from outside,

2.31  The Committee observes that the MoU rating in respect of NTPC over the last 16 years have been graded as

Power and requirement. It is a fact that NTPC is the bulk power generator in the Country. However, power supply of
country still fall short of the requirement. In view of this, excellent rating seems to be a misnomer. The Committee
therefore recommends that MoU ratio in respect of NTPC should be integrated with the actual need of the power of the
Country and production. Targets should be fixed in the national perspective.

taking several measures like reducing the number of Government Directors on the Board, and inducting professional
from finance and technology side to improve its efficiency but there is still scope for improvement although the

competitiveness MoU parameters for NTPC should be modified to raise it to the status of the global Company that

CHAPTER-IV
POWER GRID CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED (PGCIL)
4.0    PGCIL is the largest and best managed transmission utilities in the world. It was incorporated in October, 1989 for
establishment and operation of regional and national power grids, through transfer of transmission assets and manpower
from the constituent central sector undertakings namely NTPC, NEPC, NFEPCO etc. PGCIL started commercial
operation in 1992-93 and now the Company owns and operates about 46,245 ckt kms of transmission lines at 765 kV,
400 kV, 220 kV & 132 kV levels and 79 sub-stations with transformation capacity of about 44,736 MVA. The
transmission system availability is maintained consistently over 98.5% by deploying best Operation and Maintenance
practices at par with the global standards. About 40% of total power generated in the country, more than 200 billion
units worth Rs.40,000 crore per year, is being transmitted across the country over PGCIL’s transmission network.
PGCIL has been accorded ‘Mini Navratna’ status w.e.f. 14th October, 1998.
4.1    PGCIL has an impressive track record of financial performance as well. The turnover went up from a modest
Rs.634 crore in 1992-93 to Rs.2,533 crore in 2002-03, registering an average annual growth rate of 26%. It registered a
net profit of Rs.643 crore in 2002-03 as against Rs.236 crore in 1992-93 thereby establishing an annual growth rate of
about 16%.
4.2    PGCIL has in-house expertise in all specialised areas of power transmission with systems upto 800 KV EHV AC,
± 500 KV HVDC, Gas Insulated Sub-stations, Static Var Compensation, Series Capacitors, Controlled Shunt Reactors
etc. Towards dovetailing R&D activities into practice, it has tied up with various renowned Academic/Research
institutes like IITs (Indian Institute of Technology), CPRI (Central Power Research Institute), etc. Based upon its
expertise in the areas of Engineering, Contracting, Project Management, Financial management, etc., it has bagged
many national and international consultancy projects.
4.3    PGCIL has adopted one of the highly effective disaster management mechanism through deployment of
Emergency Restoration System (FRS) to minimise the adverse impact on transmission system caused by natural
calamities like flood, cyclone, earthquake etc. The devastation caused by cyclone in Gujarat in June, 1998, Orissa in
October, 1999 and earthquake in Gujarat in January, 2001 were attended by PGCIL on war footing and normalcy was
restored within few days, which otherwise would have taken several months. PGCIL has been recognized as the nodal
agency for disaster management in Indian power sector. It is the first power utility in India to evolve Environmental and
Social Policy & Procedures (ESPP) through public interactions and is implementing the ESPP in its transmission
projects in letter and spirit.
4.4    PGCIL has planned to create a strong and vibrant National Power Grid in a phased manner to ensure optimum
utilization generating resources, conservation of eco sensitive right of way and for having flexibility to accommodate
the uncertainty of generation plans. Commissioning of 500 MW Sasaram HVDC back to back link interconnecting
Eastern Region with Northern Region marked the completion of first phase of the National Grid with 5000 MW inter-
regional power transfer capacity. Under the first phase, all the power regions of the country have been interlinked
mainly through asynchronous HVDC links.
4.5    The commissioning of second phase of the National Grid has already begun with the commissioning of 2000 MW
Talcher-Kolar bi-polar HVDC link, achieved 9 months ahead of schedule and at a cost lower by Rs.700 crore than the
approved cost. Early commissioning of this project enabled transfer of surplus power from Eastern Region to Southern
Region. The 400 KV D/C Raipur-Rourkela line (East- West Interconnector) was commissioned in March 2003, thereby
enhancing the cumulative inter-regional power transfer capacity to 8000 MW. This project has been commissioned one
year ahead of schedule. Early commissioning of this line has facilitated transfer of surplus power of Eastern Region.
This also marks the synchronous operation of regional grids covering North-Eastern, Eastern, and Western Regions with
a combined installed capacity of 50,000 MW stretching from Arunachal Pradesh in North Eastern Region to Goa in
Western Region, i.e. a distance of more than 2500 KM. The second phase of National Grid consisting of a hybrid
system of HVDC & 765 kV systems shall be completed by the year 2007, when the inter-regional power transfer
capacity is envisaged to be about 23,500 MW depending upon completion of planned generation projects.

4.6    Development of National Grid would enable optimal utilization of available resources, reduction in cost of
delivered power and improve economy, reliability and quality of power supply. Further, it would benefit in terms of
reduction of generation capacity requirement due to numerous factors like time diversity, spinning reserves requirement,
improvement of hydrothermal mix etc. As per an estimate, by the year 2012 there would be reduction of about 13,000 –
MW generation addition requirements leading to saving in investment of about Rs.52,000 crore. The third phase of
National Grid would involve development of high capacity Transmission Highways comprising a ring of 765 kV lines
by the year 2012 enhancing the inter-regional power transfer capacity to the level of 30,000 MW.
4.7    For creation of such a National Grid including the evacuation system, the total investment requirement in the
central transmission sector during next 10 years has been envisaged to be about Rs.70,000 crore. Out of this, PGCIL
plans to invest to the tune of Rs.50,000 crore, while the balance of Rs.20,000 crore is envisaged to be mobilized through
Private Participation. Private investment has been envisaged through two routes, viz., Independent Private Transmission
Company (IPTC) route and Joint Venture (JV) route. PGCIL, in its attempts to encourage private participation in the
transmission sector has joined hands with private player, Tata Power for implementation of major transmission lines
associated with Tata BEP in Bhutan, costing about Rs.1,100 crore on JV route. The project with route length of around
1200 KM covers transmission lines from Siliguri (West Bengal) to Mandola (Uttar Pradesh). Kicking off the Joint
Venture, Tata Power has already picked up the 51% stake in the Shell Company viz. Tata Delhi Transmission Limited.
Such a JV shall pave the way for more such JVs thereby supplementing PGCIL’s resources and efforts. Multilateral
funding agencies like IFC & ADB shall be funding this project. In fact the IFC has decided to adopt this as a model for
seeking private participation elsewhere in the world.
4.8    The other pilot project to be taken up through IPTC route covers 400 KV double circuit transmission line from
“Bina to Nagda & Nagda to Dehgam”, and is estimated to cost Rs.450 crore, which shall be wholly owned privately.
4.9    In order to exploit the synergy of its transmission business with its inherent communication infrastructure, PGCIL
has diversified in to Telecom business. PGCIL has already initiated actions for creating backbone telecom network with
capital investment of about Rs.934 crore with funding assistance from the World Bank. The envisaged base network
shall consist of about 14,000 km of optical fibre network interconnecting 60 major Metros/Cities, which shall be
implemented by 2005. It is expected that such diversification will generate additional resources for ploughing it back to
transmission business, to augment the much needed resources to establish National Power Grid with the ultimate aim to
facilitate availability of cheaper power to the common man. PGCIL has already obtained the regulatory Infrastructure
Provider-H license from Government of India. It has already made available the telecom capacity along Delhi-Jaipur,
Delhi- Chandigarh, and Delhi- Lucknow- Mumbai corridor for commercial use by telecom service providers & has
started earning revenue for the same. PGCIL’s prestigious telecom link connecting the Capital of India, New Delhi and
Commercial Capital of India, Mumbai, was inaugurated by Hon’ble Prime Minister of India on 19.10.2002. Delhi-
Mumbai link, en-route, connects various commercial cities like Moradabad, Lucknow, Jabalpur, Itarsi, Dhule & Nasik.
4.10  Under Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programmes (APDRP) of Ministry of Power, PGCIL has
been assigned the role of Advisor-cum-Consultant to lend its managerial and technical expertise for developing 105
distribution circles. This includes 37 circles, where PGCIL is playing the direct role and in the remaining circles, which
have been developed by NPC, WAPCOS, ERDA and SFBS, the Company is acting as the coordinator. At the end of the
first phase of the programme, projects worth Rs.6,000 crore have been approved including the projects worth Rs.5587
crore, where PGCIL is associated. In addition PGCIL has also undertaken implementation of projects under APDRP
program on turnkey and bilateral basis in States like Goa & Bihar. Major projects taken up for implementation are
Renovation Modernization of Distribution systems in the circles of PESU (East), Patna and Muzaffarpur in Bihar and
North Goa in the State of Goa, Implementation of Rural Electrification Schemes in about 2600 villages in the districts of
Vaishali and Muzaffarpur in Bihar.
MoU PERFORMANCE
4.11  PGCIL has been consistently rated in the highest score of “Excellent” based on its actual performance vis-a-vis the
set forth targets in MoU signed with Ministry of Power since 1993-94. It is worth mentioning that PGCIL has the
distinction to receive the Prime Minister’s MoU Award for three consecutive years i.e. 1998-99, 1999-2000 and 2000-
2001. Based on the provisional results of performance during year 2002-03, PGCIL is poised to achieve the "Excellent"
rating for the MoU signed with Ministry of Power.

4.12  The targets included in PGCIL’s MoU may be broadly categorized into three heads, namely; 
(a) Operational targets; (b) Financial targets; and (c) Construction targets. The parameters covered under each of the
above heads are given below:
         (1)    Operational targets
                 (a)   Availability of Transmission system;
                 (b)   Number of Trippings per line attributable to PGCIL
         (2)    Financial Targets
                 (a)   Gross Margin
                 (b)   Net Profit to Capital Employed
                 (c)   Net Profit to Net worth
                 (d)   Outstanding dues beyond two months of billing cycle.
         (3)    Construction Targets
                 Stringing of Transmission Lines
4.13  After operationalisation of the MoU, PGCIL submits its quarterly performance reports to the Ministry of Power
and Department of Public Enterprises for the purpose of performance monitoring and information flow. At the end of
the financial year PGCIL submits its provisional composite score sheet to the Department of Public Enterprises and
Ministry of Power. In the MoU, in addition to parameters highlighted above, there are various other targets like, timely
signing of MoU for the current year, submission of composite score sheet for the previous year and submission of MoU
for the next year, besides targets related to Human Resource Development and application of IT, etc. Department of
Public Enterprises then evaluates the composite score sheet with audited results submitted by PGCIL and awards the
rating obtained by PGCIL.
4.14  PGCIL has been exceeding the Operational targets by maintaining transmission system availability above 98%,
which is comparable to international standards. Likewise, the financial targets and the construction targets are met
consistently for the last five years.
4.15  PGCIL, the Central Transmission Utility of the country, is playing a vital role in development of Indian Power
Sector and towards establishment of National Power Grid. PGCIL is committed to sound Corporate Governance
principles by promoting corporate fairness, transparency and accountability amongst all the stakeholders.
4.16  PGCIL, the Central Transmission Utility of the country, continued to implement its projects with economy and
within stipulated time frame to derive maximum economic benefits. Its advance and cost effective Integrated Project
Management and Control System (IPMCS) for total project review and monitoring on regular basis has contributed
significantly. Some of the initiatives taken to reduce time period of project commissioning are, advance action to
develop specifications, standardization of design and collection of project data, survey and soil investigation,
undertaking tendering activities, in parallel with project approval process, etc. These proactive measures taken by
PGCIL have led to substantial savings in terms of time and money to PGCIL in particular and the nation at large.
During the financial year 2002-2003, PGCIL commissioned projects worth Rs.3.00 crore. These projects were
completed at a cost lesser by Rs.850 Crore than the Government approved cost and major projects were completed 3 to
9 months ahead of schedule. Major transmission projects commissioned include, 500 MW Sasaram HVDC back-to-
back, ±500 MV Talcher-Kolar HVDC Bi-pole, 400 kV D/c Kolhapur-Mapusa line, 400 kV S/c Jamshedpur-Rourkela,
400 kV D/c Raipur-Rourkela line, and 400 KV Dic Vijayawada- Nellore-Chennai, etc. The Company established two
new 400/220 kV and HVDC sub-stations in the year, besides extension of many existing sub-stations.
4.17  In order to remain a premier organization in transmission business and to offer best services to the beneficiary
utilities, PGCIL has endeavoured to adopt latest technologies available in the World. Transmission lines were updated

and upgraded by utilising modem technologies. Application of Flexible AC Transmission (FACT) on 400 kV line at
marginal cost has led to 25% increase in its power transfer capacity. Further, high temperature endurance conductors,
Compact Towers, alternate type of tower structures like Guyed Structures, Pole Structures etc are also under various
stages of developmental application for enhancing power transfer capacity as well as conservation of Right-of-Way and
reduction in transmission tariff. In-house standardization of tower designs contributed not only in substantial reduction
of time in project implementation period (up to one year) but also optimizing lot of projects. PGCIL have taken up many
research and development activities in association with reputed research bodies like CPRI, IITs etc. and encouraged
Indian manufacturers to develop product, which would reduce dependence on offshore supplies.
4.18  PGCIL has made remarkable strides in the area of Information Technology both in terms of overall Improvement
in IT deployments and usage within the organization thereby increasing efficiency and communication.
4.19  PGCIL, first among the power utilities in the country, implemented State-of the Art Video Conferencing Facility
as its Corporate and Regional Offices, which is extensively utilised to organize virtual meetings and follow-up actions
leading to substantial monetary savings and traveling time of senior executives. Some of the other salient applications
are Web based Enterprise wide Information Portal as a step towards E-Governance, Inspection Management System on
internet based B2B platform and Enterprise wide Converged IT and Communication System.
4.20  PGCIL as a leading power utility committed to effective Quality Management aligned its documented Quality
Management System to the requirements of ISO-9001: 1994 version and achieved certification in July 1995. PGCIL
happens to be the first utility in Indian power sector to be bestowed with this distinction of becoming ISO-9001 certified
Company when it was certified by NVs Electricity Association Quality Assurance (EAQA) accredited by United
Kingdom Accreditation Services (UKAS), UK Re-certification of ISO-9001 standard has been carried out form time to
time incorporating structural changes as required by certified organization. POV;ERGRID has already established its
QMS with the latest version of ISO 9001/2000 way ahead of others in power sector.
4.21  The Committee during its visit to Chennai on 21st September, 2003 had extensive interaction with the
representatives of PGCIL, on its MoU performance and various parameters assigned. The Committee was impressed
with the achievements of the organisation both in terms of financial and physical parameters. The Committee was
informed that PGCIL has been performing in the area of project management which has resulted in the successful
completion of several projects ahead the scheduled time thereby saving the cost. The Committee appreciated their
performance is the case of Talchar Project.
4.22  The Committee observes that the lengthy procedure in the process of approval of projects and the delays involved
should be minimized which is a severe constraint in the functioning of any PSUs in terms of MoU. The Committee
stressed that the Government should simplify the procedure involved to avoid the delay in approval of national level
projects.
4.23  The Committee was also informed that the projects undertaken by the PGCIL utilise 80% of indigenous products
and nearly 20% of the spares are imported which involves imposition of customs duty and it adversely affects the list of
projects. The representatives of PGCIL apprised the Committee that the import duty has been adversely affecting
PGCIL and exemption should be given to them as ‘The case of BHEL which is given in terms of mega projects.
4.24  The Committee, therefore recommends that the case of PGCIL should be sympathetically considered by the
Government for import duty exemption on the lines of BHEL which is given in terms of Mega project.
4.25  The Committee also observes that the further growth potential in the core area of EHV transmission should
be fully utilized by the Government and thereby the target of National Grid would be achieved by the year 2012.
4.26  The Committee further observes that the potentials in the area of long distance communication and use of
optic fibre and state of the art technology should be fully exploited.
4.27  The Committee was apprised about the transmission loss which is 4.5% at par with the world standard. However,
the distribution loss is pinching the power sector as a whole, which is at 40% against the 5 to 8% of the world standard.
It was also stated that the load factor in the North-South was more and the East-West was less causing the trippings and
grid failures.
4.28  The Committee observes that such losses can be reduced by better management and adopting the state of
art the technology available in the global arena. The Committee further observes that the role of State Electricity
Boards can not be ruled out in achieving the speedy implementation of the ongoing distribution reform
programmes.

4.29  As regards the disaster/calamity and stress management skill available with the PGCIL the Committee appreciated
the role played by it in restoration of transmission systems in the States of Orissa and Gujarat during the national
calamity in record time.
4.30  The Committee gathers a very good impression of the performance of PGCIL in terms of MoU parameters as well
as physical and financial parameters. Further the Committee expresses that keeping in view of the achievements of
PGCIL the Government should look into the demand of PGCIL to accord ‘Navratna’ status to it. The Committee
strongly supports this demand of PGCIL.
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
         The Committee observes that the MoU rating in respect of NTPC over the last 16 years have been graded as
excellent this kind of rating needs to be modified in view of the power scenario in the country. i.e. Gross generation of
Power and requirement. It is a fact that NTPC is the bulk power generator in the Country. However, power supply of
country still fall short of the requirement. In view of this, excellent rating seems to be a misnomer. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that MoU ratio in respect of NTPC should be integrated with the actual need of the power of the
Country and production. Targets should be fixed in the national perspective.                                                             (Para
: 2.31)
         The Committee observes that although NTPC have taken measures to attain optimum growth of the Company by
taking several measures like reducing the number of Government Directors on the Board, and inducting professional
from finance and technology side to improve its efficiency but there is still scope for improvement although the
Company has a happy experience of working along the MoU instrument. In view of the increasing global
competitiveness MoU parameters for NTPC should be modified to raise it to the status of the global Company that
NTPC needs to attain in the present scenario of liberlisation of
economy.                                                                                   (Para : 2.32)
         The Committee observed that the growth criteria for power generation under MoU should be measured year after
year and not from what it was since its inception i.e. 1998-99 if the growth percentage is based from year to year, the
growth trend of this Company is not very encouraging. It is reflected in the gross generation and the total requirement of
the power in the Country. MoU system should be framed in such a way so as to exhibit growth trend year after year and
encourage and invite it. Projects should be completed with in a fixed time frame.                                        (Para : 2.34)
         The Committee observes that notwithstanding the excellent performance and improvement in the generation of
power, human productivity index should be evaluated in terms of international scale. In the Indian context, human
productivity index may be excellent but this should be comparably to average human productivity at the global scene.
MoU parameters should see to it that human productivity can be raised to optimum level and may be brought at par with
the international standards.         (Para : 2.36)
         As regards the environmental criteria where NTPC has qualitative parameters in which the main parameter relates
to ash utilisation. NTPC has been trying to improve ash utilisation in their plants progressively. The Committee is happy

major role in the Development of eco-friendly and eco-nurturing initiative towards environmental protection and
continued to sustainable power development in India. The committee feels that CENPEEP should be fully exploited so
as to ensure clean environment.                                                                                                                      (Para : 2.37)

DEVELOPMENT COMMISSIONER FOR SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES 
  
1.1       RECOMMENDATION  
  
            The Committee further observes that it has become extremely essential to create awareness about
India’s obligations under the WTO regime and their impact on vari ous sectors.  Having heard the
representatives of Powerloom, R eadymade garment, Pan Masala A ssociations, the Committee draws an
inference that there is some communication gap between the SIDO and SSI Associations.  Therefore, the
Committee recommends that there should be regul ar interaction between th e Government and Small
Scale Industries.  A Committee at local level should also be formed between Bankers and local chapters
of SSI Associations to sort out th eir problems relating to credit relate d issues at local level in all the
States. The local committee should give quarterly report to the Ministry of Small Scale Industries,
Ministry of Finance (B anking Division) and Department Rela ted Parliamentary Standing Committee
onIndustry.  
(Para No. 3.6)
 
Action Taken 
  
             
1.1.1    In order to have greater interaction, the Ministry of SSI is always in touch with SSI Associations/
entrepreneurs through its c ountrywide network of fiel d formations.  The Minist ry of SSI also has an
interactive portal, which is amongst the most visited websites.  The Ministry also consults stakeholders
in SSI Sector for taking any policy decision.  The consultations with Industry Associations are also held
for preparation of Pre-Budget proposals, for effecting dereservation, raising the investment limit, etc.  In 
SSI Board, a large number of SSI Associations are me mbers.  Recently, the Mini ster of SSI has written
to all the Members of Parliament  to interact with  the prospective SSI entrepreneurs to encourage them
to set up new SSI units in their re spective constituencies and also identify five Sick SSI Units fo r
rehabilitation.  
  
1.1.2    The performance of the ba nks is critically reviewed in different fora such as District
Coordination Committee/ Di strict Level Review Committee/ St ate Level Bankers’ Committee, where 
besides the representatives of RBI,  financing banks, concerned Stat e Governments participate in the
discussions.  In these fora SSI Associations are invited by the C onvenor banks.  Further, in DLRC
meetings public representatives such as local MLAs, MPs also participate in th e deliberations.  Besides,
all the above fora, issues re lating to credit flow to SSI Sector ar e also critically revi ewed at the highest
level in the Standing Advisory Committee(SAC) on flow  of institutional credit  to SSI Sector under the
chairmanship of the concerned Deputy Governor of RBI.  In the SAC, one all India and four State level
SSI Associations are members.  In addition to these, a State Level Inter-Institutional Committee (SLIIC) 
has also been set up in each State to deal with the problems of coordination for rehabilitation of sick SSI
units.  A Sub-Committee of SLIIC has also been set up wherein borro wers and concerned bankers are 
invited to discuss the concerned issues.  An institut ional mechanism also exists  at the dist rict level in
some of the States.  State Governments have formed  Sick Units’ Rehabilitation Committees headed by 
Deputy Commissioner/ District  Collector of the District to look into the reasons for sickness and
deliberate on the measures.  These Committees are expected to bri ng  in general awareness to the
problems and to curtail the growth of sickness.

1.2       RECOMMENDATION  
  
            The Committee hopes and recommends that Nati onal Small Industries Corporation would 
be able to restart its discounting of bill to help SSI Units whose dues have been stuck up with their
clients.  
(Para No. 4.7)
 
Action Taken 
  
1.2.1    NSIC earlier provided short-term financial assistance to SSIs under various financing schemes,
which also included the Bill Discounting Scheme. Unde r this scheme, bills pert aining to supplies made
by small scale units to eligible purchasers were discounted by NSIC upto specified limits.  During the
last two years, several parties to whom Bill Discounting facility  was granted became irregular in
repayment of their dues mainly due to non-payment of bills by the buyer’s organizations some of which 
were State Enterprises like Electrici ty Boards etc.  While finalizing the Business Restructuring Plan o f
NSIC, Govt. had directed the Corporation to phase  out the financial scheme s of the Corporation by
01.4.2007 except those for Technology Upgradation and Marketing Promotion.  
  
1.2.2    In view of the above reasons, as a first step  in this direction, the Corporation discontinued the
business of Bill Discount ing Scheme w.e.f. 01.4.2003.  However,  as desired by the Parliamentary
Standing Committee, the proposal to restart the disc ounting of bills to help SSI units whose dues have
been stuck up with their clients, will be evaluated again.

            The Committee recommends that more emphasis should be laid on research studies to 
know the lacunae hinderin g the growth of National Sma ll Industries Corporation so as to stop its
declining influence. 
(Para No. 4.8)

Restructuring of NSIC.

VENTURE CAPITAL FUND 
  
1.6       RECOMMENDATION  
  
            The Committee recommends that more Venture funds should be set up for information
technology, biotechnology and food processin g.  The Committee feels that  Venture Capital could
be a successful concept in brin ging out the latent entrepren eurship spirit of the youth of the
country.  In this context, the Committee recommends that a suitable polic y framework ma y be
designed expeditiousl y to promote settin g up of such funds in the p ublic as well as the private
sector.  Banks should be encouraged to entertain Venture Capital funding to SSI units.  
 
(Para No. 8.3)
  
Action Taken 
  
1.6.1    To encourage Venture Capital funding to SSI units banks have been a dvised that investment in
venture capital will be elig ible for inclusion in prio rity sector lending.  This is subject to the condition
that the venture capital funds/compani es are registered with SEBI.  Investment in venture capital if any,
is required to be reported separately in the half yearly return on priority sector lending, submitted to
RBI.   
  
  
ANTI DUMPING MEASURES 
  
1.7       RECOMMENDATION  
  
            The Committee observes that the major option for limiting imports that remains for use by
policy-makers in a QR-free regime is that of higher tariffs.  The Committee recommends that QRs
may be converted into tariff and non-tariff equivalents to give an adequate protection to the
domestic SSIs.  While this measure would be a discouraging factor for foreign producers to export
their cheap goods to India, it would also mean increasing revenue for the Government of India.  
 
(Para No. 12.8)
  
Action Taken 
  
  
1.7.2    Protection to the industrie s is available in the form of raising custom du ties upto the bound
levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards measures in case of surge in imports, etc. 
  
1.7.3    Under the WTO Agreements, QRs have b een abolished on many pr oducts. These have been
converted into tariffs. Some of the Non-tariff equivalents exercised by India are:  
  
1. All consignments of edible oils and processed f ood products, containing beef  in any form are not 
allowed.  
  
2.      Imports of meat and poultry pr oducts, all primary agricultural products, textile and textile
articles, alcoholic beverages, all such edible/food products, dom estic sale and manufacture o f
which are governed by Prevention of Food Adu lteration Act, 1954, Meat and Meat Products o f
all kinds etc. would be allowed under the compliance of specific Laws/Orders.

SICKNESS IN SSI SECTOR 
  
1.11     RECOMMENDATION  
  
  
            In order to revive sick industries, the Committee recommends that 
  
I.                    A special fund may be created for rehabilitation of sick SSIs and the commercial banks may 
earmark a portion of loans to ailing SSIs.  
II.                 The State Level Inter Instituti onal Committees (SLIICs) need to be revitalized and DICs 
may be used as a forum to redress the grievances regarding delays in rehabilitation. 
III.               Local Committees should be formed between the State Government and SSI Association
and Banks to sort out the credit related issues at local level.  
IV.              The Committee reiterates its observations given in its 75th Report that an Arbitration Clause 
may also be included in all borrower-lender arra ngements in terms of I ndian Arbitration Act 
to avoid protracted litigation and costs.  Although Entrepreneurship Development through
small enterprises is basicall y owner-managed, a significant  number of them do employ 
persons for performing manageri al functions.  The SSI unit s on the growth path should
encourage their key personnel to think and work more as entrepreneurs than as mere
employees.  
(Para No. 13.4)
  
Action Taken 
  
  
1.11.1  For rehabilitation of sick SSI units, RBI had set up a Work ing Group on Rehabilitation of such
units under the Chairmanship of Shri S.S.Kohli, the then Chairman of Indian banks’ Association. Based 
on the accepted recommendations of the Working Group, the RBI has drawn up the Revised Guidelines
for Rehabilitation of sick SSI units, which were ci rculated to all Scheduled Commercial banks on 16 th
January, 2002.  
  
I.          These Guidelines include broad parame ters for grant of relief an d concessions for revival o f
potentially viable sick SSI units.  The  loans extended to the ailing SSI units carry various concessions 
as given below: 
  
(a)                Working Capital – Interest 1.5% below the prevailing fixe d/prime lending rate, whereve r 
applicable. 
(b)               Funded Interest Term Loan – Interest free. 
(c)                Working Capital Term Loan – Interest to be  charged 1.5% below the prevailing fixed/prime
lending rate, wherever applicable. 
(d)               Term Loan – Concessions in the interest to be given not more than 2% (not more than 3% in

(e)                Contingency Loan Assistance – The conces sional rate allowed for Working Capital

(f)                 Additional Working Capital – Interest rates now exceeding PLR. 
  
II.         To make SLIIC more effective various measures have been taken su ch as  a  Sub-Committee o f

III.       An institutional mechanism also exists at the district level in so me of the States.  State

Commissioner/District Collector of the District.  Th e reasons for sickness in the sector are also being

IV.       The Banking Ombudsman Scheme , 2002 which has come into effect from 14 th June, 2002 
provides for the Banking Om budsman to act as an arbitrator in  any dispute between a bank and its
constituents or between a bank and another bank, if both the parties agree for such a reference and the
value of the claim in such disput e does not exceed Rs. 10 lakh. Howeve r, insertion of an arbitration
clause in the borrower lende r arrangement in terms of  Indian Arbitration Act will require examination
from legal angle.

(Para No. 17.3)

of technological upgradation and quali ty improvement in the SSI units.  However, the impacts of these

primarily be on Technology Upgradation and Marketing Promotion.  
  
1.14.2  The Modernisation of SIDO Workshop Scheme is an ongoing plan scheme with the allocation of

(Para No. 3.5)
  
Action Taken 
  
3.1.1    The role of the Development Commissioner is  that of the advocacy a nd facilitation of the SSI
Sector in the country.  With the aim to make the SSI Sector globall y and domestically competitive, a
Comprehensive Policy Package was announced in August, 2000 by the Hon’ ble Prime Minister in the
First National Convention on SSIs.  This Package cont ains measures related to credit and fiscal support,
marketing, infrastuctural development, technological  upgradation and quality im provement etc. in the
form of incentives and financial a ssistance.  With a view to obtain latest information on various aspects
of the SSI Sector, Office of the Development Commissioner (Small  Scale Industries) has conducted the
Third Census of SSIs.  The results of the Census would be utilized for policy formulation.  The Ministry
of SSI also entrusts St udies to various eminent Research In stitutes/Organisations on topical issues
pertaining to SSI sector. The findings of the Studies provide a vital feedback for Policy decisions.   
  
3.1.2    The role of Development Commissioner is reoriented from time to  time in accordance with
emerging needs.  While taking any policy initiative/decision, the DC (SSI) assures that due consultations
are held with the stakeholders in  the SSI Sector. Recently, the Deve lopment Commissioner’s Office has 
extended due focus on development of Clusters aime d at not only technological  upgradation but also to
improve credit availability in the Clusters.  A list of 60 identified Clusters has been submitted to Reserve
Bank of India for improving the flow of credit therein.  
   
  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION 
  
  
3.1.3    The Committee further obs erves that Comprehensive Polic y Packa ge was announced in
August, 2000 by the Hon ’ble Prime Minister shou ld be monitored from time to time and an y 
lacunae in this re gard should be appropriatel y removed. The Committe e also recommends that
the involvement of SSIs in Policy formulation should be done at the earliest. 
  
PROMOTION OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES SCHEMES 
  
3.2       RECOMMENDATION

            The Committee feels that techni cal assistance alongwith ot her basic necessary inputs fo r
production such as power, fuel, raw materials and credit at reasonable prices should be provided to make
SSIs more competitive.  The Committee further r ecommends that Cluster-w ise tool rooms and CAD-
CAM rooms should be set up.  
(Para No. 5.4)
  
Action Taken 
  
3.2.1    Ministry of SSI have established a numbe r of Tool Room & Traini ng Centres, as autonomous
bodies, in order to provide technical, advisory and consultancy services to the industries particularly the
small scale industries in the fields of designing, de veloping and manufacturing tools, dies, moulds, jigs,
fixtures, gauges etc. and also to provide training for tool makers. 
  
3.2.2    In order to meet the growi ng demand of tools and dies , it has been decided to persuade the State
Governments to set up Tool Rooms of smaller size (Mini Tool Room and Training Centres) with Central
assistance, which is equal to 90% of the cost of machinery, in ca se of new projects, and 75% of the cost
of  machinery in case  of existing projects to be upgraded/modernized.  The balance cost of machinery,
the cost of land, buildings and the recurring cost  are to be borne by th e State Government/State
Agencies.  This scheme was introduced w.e.f. 1.3.2001, and Government have  approved five proposals
so far received from Government  of Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Karn ataka, Nagaland and West Bengal. 
The State Governments while selecting the site of the project do take into consideration the fact that the
tool room and training facilities and CAD/CAM ar e established in the same areas where there is cluste r
of industries.  
  
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION 
  
3.2.3    The Committee further reco mmends that the Government s hould monitor the progress of the 
proposals received from the State Governments like  Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Nagaland and
West Bengal for setting up Mini Tool rooms a nd Training centres. The Government should also
persuade other State Governments to take initiative in this regard so as to spread the benefits at
macrolevel. 
  
CREDIT TO SSI SECTOR 
  
3.3       RECOMMENDATION  
  
  
            The Committee feels that the proce ss of liberalization has expose d the Small Scale Industries
(SSI) Sector to intensified compet ition both globally and dom estically.  In order to help building up the
capabilities of the units in the SSI sector to fa ce the emerging challenges, there has to be a furthe r
increase in the flow of financial assistance to facili tate additional capacity generation, expansion of the
existing units and improving thei r capacity utilization, diversif ication and to enhance the
competitiveness of the sector with a thrust on technology upgradation and modernization.  
(Para No. 6.8)
Action Taken 
  
3.3.1    As a result of globalisation/liberalizat ion of Indian economy since 1991 and recent WTO
agreements, the SSI Sector has been facing lot of competition and challenges from MNCs and the large
sector.  The solution to overcome these challenge s lies in technology upgradation, modernization,
emphasis on core competence and prom oting clusters/industrial estates.  To facilitate this, besides the
“Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme” of Small Industrie s Development Bank of India, Ministr y of

National Programmes of Cluster Development with UNIDO assistance for Toys, Locks, Machine Tools,

FURTHER RECOMMENDATION 
  
3.3.2    The Committee feels that th e Government should play a pro -active role in disseminating

technical know how.

            The Committee is of the opinion that due to locational disadvantage  and peculiar set up of the
North Eastern region, industries which have set up for full fl edged establishments in the North Eastern
Region should be given the benefit of Excise Duty  exemption to generate employment in the region. 
The Committee notes that Finance Mini ster informed th e Rajya Sabha on 6 th May, 03 that some legal 
questions had arisen regarding chewing tobacco – The Finance Minister assured the House that he

Action Taken 
  
4.1.1    The Banking Division, Ministry of Finance examined the Recommendation of the Committee in

commercial activity which has high ri sk and at the same time scope for high returns. This therefore,
cannot be termed as a social activity which need s Government support. SIDB I has been making profits

4.1.2    The recommendation regardi ng restoration of tax exemption status of SIDBI was examined in
consultation with Central Board of  Direct Taxes.  Department of Revenue feels that exemptions from
Income Tax have become inconsistent with the pr esent day moderate tax-regime and are being phase d 
out as a matter of policy. Withdrawal of tax exem ption status to SIDBI was announced in the Budget

4.1.3    Furthermore, the activities carried out by SIDBI, include comm ercial activities such as direct

in the nature of charitable  or non-profitable.  It is not out of pl ace to mention that SIDBI has earned net
profit of Rs. 405 crores and Rs. 315 crores respectively in the year s 2001-02 and 2002-03.  Considering 
all these aspects, it would not be possible to restore the tax exemption status enjoyed by SIDBI till 2000-
01.

1.3  Role of DPE in evaluation  of  MOU System 
  
The Committee recommends that DPE should reor ient and reorganise its  activities as far as
signing of MOU is concerned.  The si gning of MOUs should not be a me re formal exercise.  DPE needs
to reassess and revaluate its role in so far as  MOU is concerned. The Co mmittee further, recommends
that the signing of MOU sh ould continue to be with DPE with a view to have uniform method o f
evaluation of CPSEs. 
                                                                                                                        (Para No. 7.6)
ACTION TAKEN 
1.3.1   The MOU system is bei ng implemented since 1987-88 and during this period a number o f 
changes has taken place which aff ected the over all economic and bus iness environment both in the
domestic and international market. Keeping in view the changing e nvironment, DPE has made certain
efforts to make the MOU system a dynamic mech anism to evaluate the performance of the
managements of the PSEs. As a pa rt of these efforts emphasis was laid on dynamic para meters such as
marketing, modernisation, technol ogical upgradation, quality control,  customers satisfaction and R&D
etc.  to ensure that PSEs not onl y strengthen their operations over a long period of time but also face the
challenges of market economy.  The PSEs have alre ady been instructed to adopt international
benchmarks of efficiency and quality in their respect ive areas of operations so  that their comparative
evaluation is not only confined to th eir past performance but also reflects their standing as compared to
the other players in the market. The working of MOU System, the choice of performance criteria and the
allocation of weight to di fferent performance parameters is bei ng reviewed and suitable changes would
be incorporated from next year.

2.1  Financial performance as the main criteria for rating their achievement 
  
MOU should have relation to financ ial well being of a PSEs.  Fi nancial parameters are must to
evaluate the state of health of a PSE.  However, the Committee observes that PSEs which are even under
performing are graded as good, very good or excelle nt depending upon the level of their achievements

a way as they can create self-employment in the smal l scale sector and avail th e benefit of the schemes 
like PMRY, REGP etc. in the small and tiny se ctor. Counselling, retraini ng and redeployment ( CRR)
scheme has now taken roots.  The Co mmittee feels that there is an urge nt need to increase its spread to
cover at least 40, 000 workers per a nnum in addition to covering a back log of about 1 lakh workers.  In
this context, the Committee recomm ends that steps are urgently requi red for allocation of funds for the
scheme which needs to be at leas t doubled.  Ministry of Heavy Industries should al so ensure that PSEs

3.5.3  The Committee is of the view that the professionalisation of Board of Directors  is the sine-qu-non

segments of society i.e. public men, technocrats., mana gement experts posses a question mark on the
efficiency and effectiveness in the decision making of corporate go vernance. The Board of Directors
should be a body of expert s having in depth understanding of the global corporate rules and practices of
managerial  skill in order to obtain the global standard  of corporate governance.  Therefore, the
Committee’s  apprehension of  the nomination of part time Directors on the Board of Directors does not
come to the expectations of working of corporate world.  That is why the Committee recommends that
the Department of Public Enterprises in consulta tion with the Department of Company Affairs should
chalk out the alternative arrangement of  non-official part-time director s for generating better corporate 
governance in the PSEs.

            The Committee observes that power  manufacture sector account s for major business of BHEL
(70%) apart from Industry (20%) and international ma rket (10%).  There is a great potential in powe
r
sector due to gap between demand and supply of pow er.  But due to low investment, projects are not

Central Electricity Regulatory Commission/State Electricity Regulatory Co mmission (CERC/SERCs),
reducing Transmission   & Distribut ion (R&D) losses etc., are expected  to improve investment in this
sector and also to fill up the gap between demand and supply of power.

2.2       Photo Sensitive Goods 
The Committee recommends that the DHI should vigorously pursue the matter with Ministry of Finance.
                                                                                                                        (PARA 23.2) 
ACTION TAKEN   
2.2.1    The matter was taken up wi th Ministry of Finance for pr oviding various duty concessions.
However, Ministry of Finance, have not agreed to the proposal because of the following:-     
 (a)       Increase in Customs duty on semi finished photographic goods. 
The suggestion to increase th e Basic Customs duty on semi-fin ished photographic goods to 40% fo r 
importers other than Integrated ma nufacturers (presently HPF is the only Integrat ed manufacturer) goes
against the Central Government’s commitment to progr essively reduce the peak rate of Basic Customs 
duty. Duty increase will also have an adverse impact  on the user industries, apart from hurting a large
number of professional photographers as well as a large segment of public. 
  
(b)               Reduction in Customs duty on raw materials only for Integrated  manufacturers.  
  
            The other Raw materials like Po lyester Subbed base (for all photo-goods), base paper fo r 
manufacture of B&W printing paper,  cellulose triacetate, silver and organic ch emicals & sensitizers
attract peak rate of Customs dut y (except silver whic h attracts specific ra te of Rs. 500 per kg.).
Exemption on Silver will not be feas ible as its use in this industry is miniscule compared to its othe r
uses. Grant of end-used based ex emption only to the Integrated ma nufacturers, would be against the 
principle of horizontal equity and policy of rationalization, besides being administra tively difficult and
prone to misuse. 
  
(c) Reduction in excise duty. 
            Reduction of excise duty is not goi ng to benefit HPF in any way, since the benefit of reduced

RECOMMENDATION 
  
3.1       Plan Outlay 
  
            The Committee is constrained to note that the expenditure incurred during last year was less than
30 percent of approved outlay.  The Committee considers the informati on supplied by the DHI
incomplete in as much as it does not spell out th e reasons/circumstances explaining why there was such
a low release of the fund.  The Committee impresse s upon the DHI to provide the said information in
their ATNs, so that Committee can look into the issue and suggest remedial measures. 
                                                                                                                        (PARA 2.2) 
ACTION TAKEN  
3.1.1    Against the provision of Rs. 100 crore under Plan in BE 2002-2003, an amount of Rs. 29.20 
crore was provided under the Reve nue Section and balance Rs. 70.80 cr ore under the Capital Section o f
the Demand. However, an expenditure  of Rs. 47.95 crore only was incurr ed during the year against this
provision owing to the reason that most of th e PSEs under Department of  Heavy Industry are unde r
Disinvestment and it is not consid ered prudent by the Government to make heavy capital investment in
these PSEs. Also, a number of PSEs are carrying unspent balances from the previous years due to which
further funds could not be released during the year. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION  
3.1.2    The Committee is of the vi ew that the revival of the PSEs ca n not be linked wi th the conditions
of the disinvestments which is genera lly put off due to legal and politi cal wrangles.  Since the PSEs are
itself bleeding, keeping them on wait further would mean ciphering off last ounce of blood where the
disinvestments process would hardly extract substantial proceeds.   
RECOMMENDATION 
3.2              Allocation of more plan funds for the PSEs 
            The Committee finds that though the projections of the PSEs were  higher, only limited support
was provided by the Government.  The Committee, ther efore, recommends that allocation of more plan
funds for the PSEs may be made by the Government so that these funds coul d be utilized for capital
investment in various PSEs of the De partment of Heavy Industries.  In view of the resource crunch, this
assistance could be given in the form of working capital, non-plan lo an, government guarantee etc.  The 
Committee also impresses upon the Government to  fully utilize the funds provided and avoid the
previous years experience in this regard. 
                                                                                                            (PARA 2.4)
ACTION TAKEN  
3.2.1    Based on the requirement of funds of PSEs for capital i nvestment 2003-2004 this Department 
had projected a requirement of Rs. 214.10 crore as budgetary suppor t. However, Planning Commission
approved a budgetary support of Rs . 100 crore for 2003-2004. If necessa ry, further funds will be 
requested at RE stage. As most of the PSEs are either loss making/sick or are under reference to BIFR or
in the process of disinvestment, it  is not considered prudent by the Government to make heavy capital
investment in the PSEs.  
  
3.2.2    Government have been providing non-plan budgetary support to PSEs for salary/wages, VRS 
and statutory dues based on their requirement. Also government Gu arantees have been provided,

wherever considered necessary. Adequate f unds for the purpose were  provided through budget o r

 Further Recommendation 
3.2.3    The Committee is of the vi ew that either the process of di sinvestments should be accelerated o r
the PSEs should be provided with suff icient funds for capital investment .   Sitting over the decision is
neither going to resurrect the sick PSEs nor it is goi ng to enhance the sale proceeds of PSEs through the
disinvestments rather it would increase the liability  of the PSEs towards statutory dues and payment o f
salaries.  Therefore, the Committ ee recommends that the Government should come out of slumber, the
sooner the better not only in the business interest of the PSEs but also in the overall economic interest of
the nation.  A firm policy with effe ctive implementation is required at the moment.  It’s a now or neve r 
situation.  The Government must expedite its policy decisions without further delay.

            The Committee expresses its concer n over the under-utilization of the amount earmarked for the

alongwith the steps taken or being ta ken to promote the utilization  of  funds. N.E region is an important

out both short-term and long-term development schemes for that re gion and apprize the Committee o f
